chapters.title: Dedication: To the Republic of Geneva
paragraphs: Magnificent, most honored, and sovereign lords: I am convinced that only a virtuous man can offer his country tributes she would not blush to accept. For thirty years I have worked to make myself worthy of paying you public homage, and now that this fortunate occasion has arrived to make up in part for what my efforts could not achieve, I decided I could rely on the zeal that drives me rather than on any title that entitles me to approach you in this way. I was lucky enough to be born among you. How, then, could I reflect on the equality that nature has established among human beings, and on the inequality they have added themselves, without thinking of the deep wisdom with which both have been blended in your state? Together they work in a way that departs least from natural law while serving society best, preserving public order and guarding each person's private happiness. When I looked into the soundest principles that good sense could lay down for the constitution of a perfect government, I was so struck to find every one of them realized in yours that, even if I had not been born inside your city, I would have judged myself bound to dedicate this portrait of human society to the people who, in my judgment, enjoy its benefits most fully and have been best protected against its smallest abuses.

If I had been free to choose the place of my birth, I would have chosen a society of a size matched to the limits of human ability, that is, to the possibility of being well governed. Each member would be able to handle his own work so fully that he would never need to hand his responsibilities over to others. In such a state everyone would know everyone else so well that neither the hidden schemes of vice nor the quiet modesty of virtue could get past the eyes and verdict of the public. And because people would be used to seeing and knowing one another, each citizen's love of his country would be a love of its people rather than of its soil.

I would have wanted to be born in a country where the ruler and the citizens share one and the same interest, so that every movement of the machine would necessarily serve the good of the whole. Since that can only happen when ruler and citizens are one and the same body, I would naturally have wanted to be born under a democratic government, sensibly moderated.

I would have chosen to live and die free, which means being subject to the laws in such a way that neither I nor anyone else in the society could throw off their honorable yoke. This is a healthy and gentle yoke, and the proudest necks bear it all the more meekly because they were made to carry no other.

So I would have wanted no member of the state to be able to boast of standing above its laws, and the state to have no reason to fear being forced to accept laws from outside. For whatever the constitution of a government may be, if even one man in it is exempt from the laws, everyone else is necessarily at his mercy. And where there are two heads, one native and one foreign, however well they divide sovereign authority between them, both cannot possibly be obeyed as they should be, nor can the government to be run well.

I would not have wanted to belong to a recently founded republic, however good its laws. Its government might well have been shaped differently from what the present emergencies demand, and I could not be sure it would not be shaken and destroyed almost at birth, either because the new administration did not suit the citizens or the citizens did not suit the new administration. Liberty is like those rich and hearty foods, or those strong wines, that nourish and strengthen robust constitutions used to them, but overwhelm, upset and ruin weak and delicate bodies that have never had them. Once people are accustomed to masters, they can never again do without them. The harder they struggle to throw off their chains, the further they stray from the paths of liberty, because they mistake for liberty an unlimited license that is its exact opposite, and nearly always end up the slaves of impostors who, instead of lightening their chains, make them far heavier than before. Even the Romans, who later became the model for all free states, were unable to govern themselves when they first threw off the Tarquins. Degraded by slavery and by the shameful work those tyrants had forced on them, they were at first no better than a dull mob that had to be handled and governed with the greatest wisdom. Only so could they gradually grow used to breathing the healthy air of liberty, and these spirits, weakened or rather reduced to the level of beasts by the rod of oppression, slowly acquire the severity of character and nobility of courage that finally made them the most admirable people on earth. So I would have looked for a country that was a happy and peaceful republic, whose origin was buried in the darkness of the ages; one that had suffered only such shocks as revealed and strengthened the patriotism and courage of its members; and one whose citizens, long used to a prudent independence, were not only free but worthy of being free.

I would have chosen a country protected from the brutal rage of conquest by a fortunate inability to conquer, and, by an even more fortunate location, free from any fear of being conquered itself. It would be a free city set among nations none of which found it in their interest to attack her liberties, and all of which, on the contrary, felt it their own duty to defend those liberties when others attacked them. In a word, it would be a republic that not only held nothing to tempt its neighbors' ambition but could reasonably count on their help in case of need. A republic so well situated could fear nothing but itself. If its members trained for war, it would be to keep alive that martial ardor and generous spirit which suit liberty so well and nourish a taste for it, not because they had any need to prepare their defense.

I would have sought a country where legislative power belonged to all its inhabitants; for who can know better than the members of a society on what terms it suits them to live together? But I would not have approved of plebiscites like those of Rome, where the leaders of the commonwealth, the very people most concerned for its preservation and welfare, were shut out of the deliberations on which its safety often depended, and where, by an absurd consequence, magistrates were deprived of rights that the humblest citizen enjoyed.

On the contrary, to put an end to self-interested, ill-considered projects and dangerous innovations, which in the end ruined the Athenians, I would have wanted no private citizen to have the right to propose whatever laws came into his head. That right would belong only to the magistrates, and they in turn would use it with such caution, and the people would approve their proposals with such reserve, and the announcement of laws would be carried out with such solemnity, that every member of the community would have time enough, before the constitution could be put at risk, to recognize that nothing makes laws more sacred and respected than great age. People soon despise laws they see altered from one day to the next, and governments that get into the habit of neglecting ancient customs in the name of imaginary improvements often bring in worse evils than those they meant to correct or prevent.

Above all, I would have avoided as inevitably ill governed a republic whose people, claiming they were able to manage without magistrates, or at best giving them only a shaky authority, imprudently kept to themselves the administration of civil affairs and the carrying out of their own laws. Such must have been the crude constitution of the first governments just as they emerged from the state of nature, and it was another of the faults that helped bring down the republic of Athens.

Instead I would have chosen a society whose individual members were content with the right to confirm their laws and to decide together, on the report of their magistrates, the most important public matters. They would set up respected courts, take care to distinguish their separate functions, and each year elect the most knowledgeable, sensible and honest men among themselves to dispense justice and run the state. In such a society the integrity of the magistrates would bear testimony to the people's wisdom, and magistrates and people would honor one another. So if some dangerous misunderstanding ever disturbed public peace and harmony, even those periods of blindness and error would show clear signs of mutual restraint and esteem and of general respect for the laws, certain omens and pledges of a sincere and lasting reconciliation.

Such, magnificent, most honored and sovereign lords, are the benefits I should have looked for in the country I chose as my birthplace. And if Providence had added to these blessings a charming setting, a mild climate, fertile soil and the loveliest scenery under heaven, then to be perfectly happy I would only ask to enjoy all these gifts in the heart of this fortunate country, living peacefully in friendly company with my fellow citizens, practicing toward them, and following their example, the duties of humanity, friendship and every other virtue, so as to leave behind the name of an honest man and a worthy patriot.

If Providence had been less kind to me, or if I had come to wisdom too late through my own reflection, and found myself dragging out a weak and languishing life in some other climate, sighing in vain for the peace and rest I had thoughtlessly given up in my youth, I would at least have kept alive in my heart the very feelings I have just described, even though I could not have put them to use in my own country. Filled with a tender and disinterested affection for my faraway fellow citizens, I would have spoken to them from the bottom of my heart, in words as close as possible to these.

My dear fellow citizens, or rather my dear brothers, since ties of blood bind us no less than our common obedience to the same laws: I take endless pleasure in being unable to think of you without thinking of all the blessings you enjoy. Perhaps not one of you values them more than I do, who have lost them. The more I consider your political and civil situation, the harder it is for me to imagine that the nature of things could allow a better one. Other governments, even when they are debating their own survival, must rely on imaginary schemes or, at best, mere possibilities. As for you, your happiness is already made and placed in your hands; you have only to enjoy it, and to be perfectly happy you need only be content with being so. Your sovereignty, won or won back at sword point and maintained for two centuries by courage and wisdom, is now fully and universally recognized. The most honorable treaties have fixed your borders, confirmed your rights and secured your peace. Your constitution is excellent and fortunate, not merely the product of profound wisdom but backed by the most respected powers. Your state enjoys the greatest calm; you have no wars or conquerors to fear; you have no masters except the wise laws you have made yourselves, enforced through upright magistrates whom you pick yourselves. You are not so rich as to be softened by luxury and lose, in the pursuit of empty pleasures, your appetite for true happiness and lasting virtue, nor so poor as to need foreign help to supplement the fruits of your own labor. In short, it hardly costs you anything to keep that precious liberty which great nations can preserve only by submitting to the most extravagant taxes.

Long may such a wisely and happily constituted republic flourish, for the happiness of its citizens and as an example to mankind! This is the only wish left for you to make, the only thing left for you to think about. From now on, the matter rests with you alone, not to make yourselves happy, since your ancestors have spared you that trouble, but to make your happiness last by using it wisely. Your survival depends on your unbroken unity, your submission to the laws, and your deference toward those who administer them. If the smallest seeds of bitterness or distrust remain among you, hurry to root them out like an accursed yeast that would sooner or later bring misfortune and ruin on the commonwealth. I urge you all to withdraw into the depths of your own hearts and consult the secret voice of your conscience. Can any one of you point to a more upright, wiser or more respectable body of men anywhere in the world than your own magistrates? Do not all of them set you a perfect example of moderation, plain living, respect for the laws and sincere reconciliation? Why, then, for your own sake, will you not give such wise superiors the unreserved confidence that virtue has a right to expect from reason? Remember that you chose them, that they justify your choice, and that the respect owed to those you have put in authority necessarily reflect on you. Is any of you so inattentive as not to see that once the laws lose their vigor and their defenders lose their authority, no one can have either safety or liberty? What is asked of you, then, except to do cheerfully and without hesitation what your interest, your duty and sound reason ought to lead you to do? Never let a blameworthy and dangerous indifference toward upholding the constitution make you neglect, whenever you need it, the prudent advice of your most knowledgeable and devoted fellow citizens. Let fairness, moderation and the most respectful firmness continue to guide everything you do, and show the whole world the example of a bold and modest people, equally jealous of its glory and its freedom. Above all, and this is the last advice I will give you, beware of malicious interpretations and poisoned talk, whose concealed motives are frequently more harmful than the actions they attack. A whole household will wake from sleep and take the alarm from a faithful, watchful dog that barks only when thieves approach; but we hate the nuisance of those noisy, troublesome curs that are forever disturbing the public peace, and whose endless, ill-timed warnings stop us from listening to the ones they occasionally give at the right moment.

And you, magnificent and most honored lords, you worthy and respectable magistrates of a free people, permit me to present you my own particular duty and homage. If there is any rank among men that can lend distinction to those who hold it, surely it is the one that talent and virtue together confer, the one you have earned and to which your fellow citizens have raised you. Their merit adds greatly to the brilliance of yours. Since men who are themselves capable of governing others have chosen you to govern them, I place you as far above other magistrates as a free people, and above all the one you have the honor to preside over, is above the common mass of other states in knowledge and wisdom.

Let me mention an example that should have left better traces, one my heart will never stop thinking of. I cannot recall without the most pleasant emotion the memory of the virtuous citizen to whom I owe my life, and who often taught me, in my childhood, the respect owed to you. I seem to see him still, earning his bread by the work of his hands while feeding his mind with the loftiest truths. I see Tacitus, Plutarch and Grotius lying mixed in with the tools of his trade. Next to him I see a beloved son receiving, alas, with far too little profit, the tender instruction of the best of fathers. Though the follies of a thoughtless youth made me forget those wise lessons for a time, I have at last the happiness of knowing that however inclined to vice a pupil may be, it is almost impossible that he will not one day or another benefit from the education given him by a truly affectionate teacher!

Such, magnificent and most honored lords, are the citizens, indeed even the common natives, of the country you govern. Such are these knowledgeable and sensible men, about whom, under the labels of tradesmen and common people, other nations are used to forming the meanest and falsest ideas. My father, I admit it gladly, was not at all remarkable among his fellow citizens; he was simply what they all are. Yet such as he was, there is no country where his conversation would not have been sought after, and where men of the highest rank and fortune would not have cultivated his acquaintance, to their considerable benefit. It is not for me to speak to you, and thank heaven there is no need, of the regard you owe to men of this kind. By education, nature and birth they are your equals; by their own choice they are your inferiors, since they gave your merit that preference, and you in turn owe them some gratitude for it. I am delighted to hear with what kindness and condescension you soften, in all your dealings with them, the gravity that suits ministers of the law; how well you repay the respect and obedience they give you with your esteem and your attention to their welfare. This conduct is full of justice and wisdom, and it increasingly erases the memory of those unfortunate events that deserve to be buried in endless silence and oblivion! It is all the more sensible because this fair and generous people takes pleasure in its duty, is naturally fond of honoring you, and finds that those most eager to defend their own rights and privileges are also the most inclined to respect yours.

It is not strange that the heads of a civil society should care for its glory and welfare. But it is an uncommon happiness when those who regard themselves as the magistrates, or better the masters, of a more sacred and loftier country show some affection for the earthly country that supports them. How pleasing it is to be able to make so rare an exception in our favor, and to count among our best citizens those devoted keepers of the sacred articles of faith that the laws have authorized, those venerable shepherds of souls, whose gentle and lively eloquence is all the better suited to planting the maxims of the Gospel in people's hearts because they are the first to show the fruits of them! Everyone knows how successfully the great art of the pulpit is practiced at Geneva. But we are so used to hearing clergymen say one thing and do another that few people stop to consider to what extent the spirit of Christianity, saintliness of life, strictness with themselves and indulgence toward their neighbors prevail throughout our body of ministers. Geneva is perhaps the only city in the world that can boast so perfect and edifying a union between its men of letters and its clergy! It is largely on their acknowledged wisdom and moderation, and on their zeal for the prosperity of the commonwealth, that I rest my hopes of its lasting tranquillity. I observe with pleasure, surprise and respect how much they abhor the appalling maxims of those sacred and barbarous men of whom history offers more than one example, who, to defend the supposed rights of the Almighty, that is, their own interests, spilled human blood the more freely because they flattered themselves that their own would always be spared.

Can I forget here that precious half of the republic, the half that creates the happiness of the other half, and whose gentleness and prudent conduct do so much to secure for it the blessings of peace and good morals? Lovable and virtuous women of my city, it will always be the fate of your sex to rule ours. Fortunate are we as long as your chaste power, confined within the bounds of married life, is exercised only for the glory and happiness of your country! This is how women held command at Sparta, and so you deserve to hold it at Geneva. What man is hard-hearted enough to refuse honor and reason when they come from the lips of a loving wife? Who would not despise the empty charms of luxury on seeing your simple and modest dress, which, because of the luster it takes from you, looks the most becoming to beauty? It is your task to keep harmony alive among citizens, with a proper love and respect for the laws of their country, through your lovable and innocent rule and your winning conversation; to reunite divided families through happy marriages; and above all to correct, through the persuasive gentleness of your lessons and the modest graces of your speech, the mistaken notions of things that our young people absorb abroad. From there, instead of any of the many useful things within reach of their observation and practice, they bring home nothing but a boyish tone and ridiculous airs learned among loose women, together with admiration for some supposed grandeur, a poor compensation for slavery, which cannot compare with the true and native greatness of august liberty. So always remain what you are now, the pure-hearted keepers of our morals and the gentle bonds of our peace, and keep exercising on every occasion the privileges of nature and the heart in the service of duty and virtue!

I hope no event will ever make me a liar for guaranteeing, on the strength of your powerful support, eternal glory to the republic and happiness to its citizens. I must admit, however, that with all these advantages our state can never claim the brilliant and dazzling appearance that catches most people's eyes, and a childish, deplorable taste for which is the deadliest foe of prosperity and freedom. Let dissolute young men run off to other countries in search of easy pleasures and long repentance. Let pretenders to good taste go and admire the splendor of palaces elsewhere, the elegance of carriages, the sumptuousness of furniture, the pomp of spectacles, together with every refinement of luxury and effeminacy. At Geneva you find nothing but men. Yet that sight has its own value, and those who look for it are fully the equal of the admirers of everything else.

Please, magnificent, most honored and sovereign lords, accept all of you with the same goodness these respectful expressions of the share I take in your common prosperity. If, in this lively outpouring of my heart, I have unhappily given way to any indiscreet transports, I humbly beg you to forgive it in view of the tender love of a true patriot and the ardent, lawful zeal of one who wishes for himself no higher joy than seeing you all happy.
With the deepest respect, magnificent, most honored and sovereign lords, I am your most humble and most obedient servant and fellow citizen, John James Rousseau. Chambéry, 12 June 1754.

chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: The most useful and least developed of all human studies is, in my opinion, the study of man, and I dare say that the inscription on the temple at Delphi contained by itself a more important and difficult lesson than all the thick volumes of the moralists. I therefore regard the subject of this Discourse as one of the most interesting questions philosophy can raise and, regrettably for us, among the knottiest that philosophers can try to settle. For how can we discover the source of inequality among men without knowing men themselves? And how can man see himself as nature made him, in spite of all the changes that a long succession of years and events must have worked on his original constitution, and tell what belongs to his own essence from what circumstances and his own progress have added to or altered in his primitive condition? The human soul is like the statue of Glaucus, which time, sea and storms had so disfigured that it resembled a savage animal more than a deity. Altered in the heart of society by a thousand ever-changing causes, by countless discoveries and errors, by changes in the make-up of the bodies around it, and by the constant clash of its own passions, the human soul has lost so much of its original appearance that it can scarcely be recognized. Instead of a being that always acts on fixed and unvarying principles, in place of the heavenly, majestic simplicity its Author stamped on it, we find only the shocking contrast of passion that believes it is reasoning and an understanding in delirium.

What is still crueler is that every improvement made by the human species only carries it further from its primitive condition, so that the more new knowledge we accumulate, the more we cut ourselves off from acquiring the most important knowledge of all. In a sense it is by studying man that we have made ourselves unable to know him.

It does not take great insight to see that the first origin of the differences between men must be sought in these successive changes in the human frame. It is generally agreed that men are naturally as equal among themselves as the animals of every species were before various physical causes produced the varieties we now see in some of them. In fact, it is impossible to imagine how these first changes, whatever caused them, could have altered all the individuals of the species at once and in the same way. Clearly, while some improved or worsened their condition and picked up various good or bad qualities that were not part of their nature, the rest stayed longer in their original state. Such was the first source of inequality among men, which it is far easier to point out in general terms than to trace back precisely to its true causes.

So my readers should not suppose that I pride myself on having seen what I consider so hard to discover. I have opened up some arguments and ventured some conjectures, not so much in hope of settling the question as to throw some light on it and to state it truly. Others will easily be able to go further along the same road, but none will find reaching the end of it easy. For it is by no means a simple task to separate what is natural from what is artificial in man's present constitution, and to become well acquainted with a state that perhaps never existed, no longer exists and probably never will, yet of which we must have sound notions in order to judge our present state correctly. Indeed, a man must be more of a philosopher than most people think to take it upon himself to say exactly what precautions are needed for making reliable observations on this subject. In my opinion, a sound answer to the following problem would not be beneath the Aristotles and Plinys of our age: what experiments would be needed to know man as nature made him, and what are the best ways to carry out those experiments within society? Far from claiming to solve this problem, I believe I have thought enough about it to dare say in advance that the wisest philosophers would not be too wise to direct such experiments, nor the most powerful rulers too powerful to carry them out. That combination of circumstances is hardly to be expected, or at least not with the perseverance, or rather the continuing supply of knowledge, insight and goodwill on both sides, that success would require.

These investigations, hard to carry out and little thought of until now, are still the only means left to us for clearing away a thousand difficulties that hide the true foundations of human society. Our ignorance of man's nature is what blurs and darkens any correct definition of natural right. As Monsieur Burlamaqui puts it, the idea of right, and even more the idea of natural right, are plainly ideas that depend on the nature of man. This great philosopher continues: it is therefore from man's very nature, from his constitution and his condition, that the principles of this science must be drawn.

It is impossible to see, without surprise and scandal, how little agreement exists on this important point among the various authors who have dealt with it. Hardly any two of the gravest writers share one opinion. Leave aside the philosophers of antiquity, who appear to have competed in contradicting each other about the most basic principles. The Roman jurists place man and every other animal under one and the same natural law, either because by that name they mean the law nature imposes upon herself more than the one she lays down for others, or, more probably, because of the peculiar sense the word "law" had for these jurists, who here seem to understand by it nothing beyond the general relations nature sets up among all living creatures for the sake of their shared preservation. The moderns, who accept as "law" only a rule given to a moral being, one that is intelligent, free, and looked at in connection with other beings, restrict the competence of natural law to the single animal gifted with reason, namely man. But each defines this law in his own manner and builds it on such abstruse metaphysical foundations that, far from being able to discover those foundations themselves, very few among us can even grasp them. So every definition offered by these learned men, though they clash on everything else, comes down to the same claim: nobody can understand the law of nature, and therefore obey it, unless he is an extremely subtle reasoner and a profound metaphysician. This amounts to saying that men, when they set up society, must have drawn on a stock of knowledge that is very hard for most people to develop, indeed impossible, even inside society.

Given how little men know of nature and how poorly they agree on what "law" means, we can hardly expect them ever to agree on a sound definition of natural law. Accordingly, all those found in books, apart from lacking uniformity, rest on many kinds of insight that men do not naturally possess and on benefits they cannot even imagine as long as they stay in the state of nature. The writers begin by asking which rules would be best, in the common interest, for men to agree among themselves; then, with no further ceremony, they apply the label natural law to a set of such rules, offering as the only proof that the collection deserves the name the benefit that universal compliance with it would bring. This is certainly a very easy way to manufacture definitions and to explain the nature of things through a nearly arbitrary fitness.

But so long as we remain ignorant of the constitution of man as he first left the hands of nature, it is pointless to try to decide what law he was given or what law fits him best. The only thing we can clearly identify about that law is twofold: for it to count as law, the will of the person it binds must submit to it with knowledge of the obligation; and for it to count as natural, it must speak immediately in the voice of nature.

So I set aside all the scholarly treatises that teach us only to look at men as they have made themselves, and confine myself to the first and simplest workings of the human soul. In it I think I can distinguish two principles that come before reason. One makes us take a deep interest in our own survival and well-being, and the other fills us with a natural reluctance to see any other being, above all any being like ourselves, suffer or die. From the cooperation and combination that our mind is able to form between these two principles, without any need to add sociability as a third, flow, in my opinion, all the rules of natural right. Reason is later forced to rebuild these rules on other foundations, when by gradually developing its powers it has finally smothered the authority of nature.

By proceeding in this way we are freed from having to make a man a philosopher before he can be a man. His obligations are not laid down for him solely by the slow voice of wisdom. As long as he does not fight the inner prompting of compassion, he will never harm another man, or even any other sentient creature, except in those lawful cases where his own survival is at stake and it is therefore his duty to put himself first. This also puts an end to the ancient disputes over whether other animals share in the law of nature. It is clear that, lacking reason and free will, they cannot know that law. But since they share to some extent in our nature through the sensitivity with which they are endowed, we may well suppose they should also share in the benefit of natural law, and that man owes them certain kinds of duty. Indeed, if I am bound not to harm any being like myself, it seems to be less because he is a rational being than because he is a sentient one; and since this quality is common to men and animals, it should at least exempt the animals from needless ill treatment by men.

This same study of primitive man, of his actual needs and the basic principles of his duties, is also the only good method for overcoming an endless number of difficulties about the origin of moral inequality, the true foundations of political bodies, the mutual rights of their members, and a thousand similar questions that are as important as they are poorly understood.

Viewed calmly and without self-interest, human society seems at first to display nothing except the violence of the strong and the oppression of the weak. The mind is horrified by the cruelty of the one and saddened by the blindness of the other. Nothing in human life is less stable than those external relations, produced by chance more often than by wisdom, that we call weakness or power, poverty or wealth; so human institutions look, at first glance, like castles built upon quicksand. Only by examining them closely, and by sweeping away the dust and sand that surround and hide the structure, do we notice the unshakable base on which it stands and come to respect it. Yet unless we study man seriously, along with his natural abilities and how they successively developed, we shall never manage to draw these distinctions or to separate, in the world as it is, what comes from the divine will from what human art claims as improvement. The political and moral reflections that the question I am examining invites are therefore valuable in every way, and the hypothetical history of governments is an instructive lesson for man in every way. Reflecting on what we would have turned into had we been left alone, we should learn to give thanks to the One whose kindly hand, by amending our institutions and giving them a firm footing, has averted the disorders that would otherwise have followed, and has caused our happiness to spring from means that, to all appearances, would without his intervention have finished off our misery.
Quem te Deus esse jussit, et humana qua parte locatus es in re, disce.

chapters.title: Exordium
paragraphs: What is the origin of inequality among mankind, and is such inequality authorized by the law of nature?

It is of man that I must speak, and the very question I am answering tells me I am speaking to men; for only those who are not afraid to honor truth have the right to raise discussions of this kind. So I will confidently defend the cause of mankind before the sages who invite me to stand up for it, and I will count myself fortunate if I can only behave in a way not unworthy of my subject and my judges.

I see two kinds of inequality among men. One I call natural or physical, because nature establishes it, and it consists in differences of age, health, bodily strength and qualities of mind or soul. The other may be called moral or political, because it depends on a sort of convention and is established, or at least authorized, by the common consent of mankind. It consists in the different privileges that some men enjoy at the expense of others, such as being richer, more honored or more powerful than they are, and even being able to demand their obedience.

It would be absurd to ask what causes natural inequality, since the bare definition of it answers the question. It would be more absurd still to wonder whether the two kinds of inequality might be essentially connected, for that would mean asking, put differently, whether people who give the orders are inevitably better than people who follow them, and whether physical or mental strength, wisdom and virtue are always found in people in proportion to their power or wealth. This is a question that might perhaps be debated by slaves within hearing of their masters, but it does not suit free and reasonable beings who are seeking the truth.

So what exactly is this Discourse about? It is to identify, in the course of events, the moment when right replaced violence and nature became subject to law. It is to lay out the chain of surprising events through which the strong came to serve the weak, and the people to buy an imaginary ease at the price of real happiness.

Every philosopher who has examined the foundations of society has felt the need to go back to a state of nature, but not one of them has ever got there. Some have not shrunk from attributing to man in that state ideas of justice and injustice, without bothering to prove that he really had such ideas, or even that they would have been useful to him. Others have talked about everyone's natural right to hold on to what is his, without saying what they understood by "his." Others again, simply handing the strongest an authority over the weakest, have immediately produced government, without considering the time men needed to form any notion of what the words "authority" and "government" mean. In short, all of them, constantly harping on needs, greed, oppression, desires and pride, have carried into the state of nature ideas collected in society. They claimed to speak of savages and described citizens. Indeed, few of our own writers seem even to have doubted that a state of nature once really existed. Yet it is plain from sacred history that even the first man, who had received instruction and commandments directly from God, never lived in that state. And if we give the books of Moses the authority that any Christian philosopher must grant them, we have to deny that such a state ever existed among men even before the Flood, unless they fell into it through some extraordinary event. That is a paradox very hard to defend and altogether impossible to prove.

Let us begin, then, by setting the facts aside, for they do not touch the question. The investigations we may undertake here are not to be understood as historical truths but only as hypothetical, conditional reasoning, better suited to explaining the nature of things than to showing their true origin, like the systems our natural scientists produce daily about how the world was formed. Religion commands us to believe that, since God himself drew men out of the state of nature, they are unequal because he wished them to be that way. Yet religion does not prevent us from making conjectures, based only on the nature of man and of the beings around him, about what would have become of mankind if it had been left to itself. That is the question I have to answer, and the one I mean to look into in this Discourse. Since my topic concerns mankind in general, I will try to use language that suits all nations. Or rather, setting aside time and place so as to think only of the people I am addressing, I will picture myself in the Lyceum at Athens, reciting the lessons of my masters before judges like Plato and Xenocrates, with the whole human race as my audience.

O man, whatever country you come from and whatever your opinions, listen to my words. You will hear your history as I believe I have read it, not in books written by people like you, who are liars, but in the book of nature, which never lies. Everything I repeat after her must be true, except where I may happen, without meaning to, to bring in my own ideas. The times I am going to speak of are very distant. How far you have changed from what you used to be! In a sense I am about to write the life of your species, from the qualities you received, which your education and your habits could corrupt but could not destroy. There is, I know, an age at which each of you would choose to stop, and you will look for the age at which, if you had your wish, your species would have stopped. Dissatisfied with your present condition for reasons that threaten your unhappy descendants with still greater dissatisfaction, you may wish you could go back. This feeling ought to be taken as praise of your first ancestors, condemnation of your contemporaries, and a source of terror to anyone unlucky enough to come after you.

chapters.title: First Part
paragraphs: However important it may be, for forming a sound judgment of man's natural state, to look at him from his origin and examine him in the first germ of the species, I will not trace his bodily organization through its successive stages toward perfection. I will not stop to ask what he may have been in the animal system at the beginning, in order to become in the end what he now is. I will not inquire whether, as Aristotle thinks, his uncut nails were at first no better than crooked claws; whether his whole body was thickly covered, like a bear's, with coarse hair; or whether, walking on all fours with his eyes on the ground and confined to a horizon a few paces wide, he thereby revealed both the nature and the bounds of his thoughts. On this topic I might only form hazy, almost fictional guesses. The science of comparative anatomy has not yet advanced far enough, and the observations of natural science are not yet well enough established, to lay the base of a solid system on such foundations. For this reason, without appealing to the supernatural information we have been given on the matter, and without paying attention to the alterations that must have occurred in the shape of his inner and outer parts as he put his limbs to new uses and took to new foods, I will suppose his build to have always been what we now see: that he always walked on two feet, used his hands as we use ours, cast his gaze over the whole face of nature, and gauged with his gaze the vast breadth of the heavens.

If I strip this being, so constituted, of whatever supernatural gifts he may have been given and of all the artificial abilities he could only have acquired slowly, and consider him, in a word, as he must have emerged from nature's hands, I see an animal that is less strong than some and less nimble than others, but on the whole better organized than any. I see him satisfying his hunger under the first oak and quenching his thirst at the first stream, lying down to sleep at the foot of the same tree that gave him his meal; and behold, all his needs are met.

Abandoned to its own natural fertility and blanketed with vast forests never marked by an axe, the earth offers food and shelter at every step to every kind of animal. Men, scattered among them, watch and imitate their skills, and so rise to the level of the beasts' instincts. They have this advantage, that while each animal species is limited to its own particular instinct, man, who perhaps has none that is specially his, takes over the instincts of all the others and feeds equally well on most of the different foods that the animals divide among themselves. This puts him in a position to find his living more easily than any of them.

Men who are used from infancy to bad weather and the harshness of the seasons, who are hardened by fatigue and forced to defend their lives and their prey, naked and unarmed, against the other wild inhabitants of the forest, or at least to escape their fury by running, develop a robust and almost unchangeable bodily constitution. Their children are born with the excellent constitution of their parents and strengthen it through the same exercises that first produced it, so that they reach all the vigor the human frame is capable of. Nature treats them precisely as Sparta treated its citizens' children: the ones born well formed she makes strong and sturdy, and she destroys the rest. In this she differs from our societies, where the state, by letting children become a burden to their parents, kills them all without distinction, even in their mothers' wombs.

Since the body is the only tool savage man knows, he puts it to many different uses of which ours, for lack of practice, are incapable; and we have our own industry to thank for the loss of the strength and agility that necessity forces him to acquire. If he had an axe, would his hand so easily break so stout a branch off an oak? If he had a sling, would it hurl a stone so far? If he had a ladder, would he climb a tree so nimbly? If he had a horse, would he race so swiftly across the plain? Allow civilized man time to collect every one of his machines near him, and he will surely defeat the savage. But if you wish to witness a contest even more lopsided, set them naked and unarmed against each other, and you will quickly grasp the benefit of having all one's forces always at one's disposal, of being constantly ready for any event, and of always carrying oneself, as it were, whole and entire.

Hobbes claims that man is naturally without fear and always eager to attack and fight. A distinguished philosopher thinks the opposite, and Cumberland and Pufendorf say the same, that nothing is more timid than man in a state of nature, that he is forever trembling and ready to flee at the first movement he notices or the first noise that reaches his ears. This may well be true of things unfamiliar to him, and I am sure that he is frightened by every new sight, whenever he cannot tell what physical good or harm to expect from it, or compare his strength with the dangers he will face. Such circumstances seldom arise in a state of nature, where everything proceeds so evenly and the surface of the earth is not exposed to the sudden, continual changes that the passions and instability of crowded communities bring about. But savage man, living among other animals with no society and no fixed home, and finding himself early obliged to measure his strength against theirs, soon makes the comparison. Finding that he beats them in skill by more than they beat him in strength, he learns to stop fearing them. Pit a bear or a wolf against a sturdy, nimble, determined savage, and and all of them are, equipped with stones and a stout stick, and you will soon find that the danger is at least equal on both sides, and that after several such trials wild beasts, which do not like to attack one another, will have little taste for attacking a creature they have found every bit as wild as themselves. Concerning animals whose strength truly exceeds man's skill, his position toward them is that of other weaker species, which manage to survive anyway. He even has this great advantage over those weaker species: being as fast as they are, and finding on every tree an almost inviolable refuge, he is always free to take it or leave it, and so to fight or flee as he pleases. We may add that no animal makes war on man by nature, except in self-defense or from extreme hunger, nor shows toward him any of those violent antipathies that seem to indicate that some species are meant by nature to be food for others.

But there are other, more formidable enemies against which man lacks the same means of defense: natural infirmities, infancy, old age and sickness of every kind. These are sad proofs of our weakness, of which the first two are shared by all animals and the last mostly afflicts man living in society. It is even notable that, as regards infancy, a mother who can carry her child with her wherever she goes can nurse it with much less trouble than the females of many other animals, who must keep going back and forth with considerable effort and weariness, one way to look for their own food and another to suckle and feed their young. True, if the woman dies, her child is in great danger of dying with her. But this danger is shared by a hundred other species whose young need a lot of time before they can look after themselves; and while our infancy lasts longer than theirs, so do our lives too, so that in this respect everything is more or less equal. There are other rules about the length of the first stage of life and the number of offspring in man and other animals, but they do not belong to my subject. With old people, who move and perspire little, the need for food declines along with their ability to obtain it. A savage life would spare them gout and rheumatism, and of all ills old age is the one that human help can least relieve, so they would finally pass away without others noticing that they had ceased to exist, and almost without noticing it themselves.

On the subject of sickness, I will not repeat the empty and false speeches most people make to discredit medicine while they are healthy. I will only ask whether there are any solid observations from which we may conclude that in countries where the healing art is most neglected, the average human lifespan is shorter than in those where it is most cultivated. And how could that be so, if we bring upon ourselves more diseases than medicine can provide cures for! The extreme inequality in the ways of life of the different classes, the excess of idleness in some and of toil in others, the ease with which we stir up and satisfy our appetites and sensuality, the over-refined and exotic dishes of the rich that fill them with burning humors and cause indigestion, the unwholesome food of the poor, which, bad as it is, they often go without, so that at every opportunity they eat greedily and overload their stomachs, late nights, excesses of every kind, uncontrolled outbursts of every passion, exhaustion, drained spirits, in short the countless pains and anxieties attached to every condition and which constantly torment the human mind: these are fatal proofs that most of our ills are our own work, and that we might have escaped almost all of them by adhering to the plain, regular and solitary life that nature laid down for us. If nature intended us always to enjoy good health, I almost dare claim that a state of reflection is a state against nature, and that the man who thinks is a depraved animal. We need only recall the good constitution of savages, at any rate of those whom we have not yet destroyed with our strong drink, and consider that they are strangers to almost every disease except those caused by wounds and old age, to be nearly convinced that the history of human diseases could easily be written by following the history of civil societies. That at least was the opinion of Plato, who concluded from certain remedies used or endorsed by Podalirius and Machaon during the siege of Troy that several disorders those remedies were known to cause in his own day were not known among men at that remote time.

In a state of nature, then, where there are so few sources of sickness, man has little need of medicine and still less of doctors, and the human species is no more to be pitied in this respect than any other animal species. Ask those who hunt for sport or for a living whether they meet many sick or feeble animals on their outings. They meet many with the marks of serious wounds that have healed and closed perfectly, many whose bones were once broken and whose limbs were almost torn off but have knit and joined completely, with no surgeon but time, no regimen but their ordinary way of living, and whose cures were no less perfect for never having been tortured with incisions, poisoned with drugs or worn down by diet and fasting. In short, however useful well-administered medicine may be to us who live in society, it remains beyond doubt that if the sick savage with no help has nothing to hope for from nature, he also has nothing to fear except his disease, a circumstance that often makes his situation better than ours.

So let us take care not to confuse savage man with the men we see and talk with every day. Nature treats all animals left in her care with a favoritism that seems to prove how protective she is of that privilege. Horses, cats, bulls, even the donkey, are usually taller, and invariably sturdier, livelier, stronger and bolder in their forests than in our houses. They lose half those advantages by becoming domestic animals; it looks as though all our care to treat them kindly and feed them well merely degrades them. The same holds for man himself. As he becomes sociable and a slave to others, he becomes weak, timid and servile, and his soft, effeminate way of living completes the weakening of both his strength and his courage. We may add that the gap between man and man in the savage and domestic conditions must be even wider than between beast and beast. Since nature treats men and beasts alike, all the comforts with which men indulge themselves more than they do the animals they tame are so many particular causes that make them degenerate more noticeably.

Nakedness, then, the lack of houses, and of all those unnecessary things we think so necessary, are no great evils for these primitive men, and much less an obstacle to their survival. Their skin, it is true, has no hair, but in warm climates they have no need of such a covering, and in cold ones they soon learn to use the skins of the animals they have overcome. They have only two feet to run on, but they have two hands to defend themselves and supply all their needs. Teaching their children to walk may cost them a great deal of time and trouble, but the mothers carry them easily, an advantage not granted to other animal species, whose mothers, when chased, must either abandon their young or adjust their pace to theirs. In short, unless we admit those singular and chance combinations of circumstances that I will discuss later, and that may very well never have occurred, it is clear in every version of the question that the man who first made himself clothes and built himself a hut gave himself things he did not much need, since he had lived without them until then. And why should he not have been able to endure in his adult years the same kind of life he had endured since infancy?

Alone, idle and always surrounded by danger, savage man must like sleep and sleep lightly, like other creatures that think little and could be said to sleep all the time they are not thinking. Since self-preservation is nearly his only concern, the faculties he exercises most must be those most useful for attack and defense, whether to overcome prey or to avoid becoming another animal's. The organs that only softness and sensuality can refine, on the other hand, must remain crude and wholly incapable of delicacy. Since his senses are split in this fashion, his touch and his taste must be extremely coarse and dull, while his sight, hearing and smell are equally keen. Such is the animal state in general, and, if we believe travelers, it is the state of most savage nations. We should not be surprised, then, that the Hottentots at the Cape of Good Hope are able to make out ships at sea with the naked eye from as far away as the Dutch manage with their spyglasses; or that the savages of America tracked the Spaniards by scent as accurately as the finest hounds would have done; or that all these barbarous nations bear nakedness without pain, use huge quantities of pepper to flavor their food, and drink Europe's strongest liquors like water.
So far I have considered man only in his physical aspect; let us now try to examine him from a metaphysical and moral point of view.

In any mere animal I see only a clever machine, to which nature has given senses so that it can wind itself up and protect itself, to a certain extent, against anything that might destroy or disturb it. I see precisely the same in the human machine, with this difference: in all the operations of the beast, nature alone acts, whereas man, as a free agent, has a share in his own. One chooses by instinct, the other by an act of freedom. For that reason the beast cannot depart from the rules prescribed to it, even where departing from them would be useful, while man often departs from his rules to his own harm. Thus a pigeon would starve beside a dish of the finest meat, and a cat beside a heap of fruit or grain, though either could perfectly well live on the food it scorns if it ever thought of trying it. In the same way dissolute men give way to excesses that bring on fevers and even death, since the mind perverts the senses, and when nature falls silent the will goes on dictating.

All animals must be admitted to have ideas, since all have senses; they even combine their ideas to a certain degree, and in this respect the difference between man and beast is merely one of degree. Some philosophers have even claimed that the difference between one man and another is greater than that between some men and some beasts. Thus it is less his understanding that marks man off from other animals as his being a free agent. Nature speaks to every animal, and beasts obey her voice. Man feels the same impulse, but he also knows that he is free to resist or to give in, and it is above all in his consciousness of this freedom that his soul's spirituality shows itself. For natural science explains to some degree the workings of the senses and the formation of ideas, but in the capacity to will, or rather to choose, and in the awareness of that power, we find only acts that are purely spiritual and cannot be explained by the laws of mechanics.

But even if the difficulties that surround all these questions left some room to dispute this difference between man and beast, there is another very distinctive quality that separates them, and one that cannot be disputed. It is the capacity for self-improvement, which, as circumstances allow, develops all the other faculties in turn, and which resides in us not only as a species but in each individual. A beast, by contrast, is, after a few months, everything that it will ever be for the rest of its life, and its species after a thousand years is just what it had been in the first year of that long period. Why is man alone liable to senility? Is it not because he thereby returns to his primitive condition? While the beast, which has acquired nothing and so has nothing to lose, always keeps its instinct, man loses through old age or accident everything his perfectibility had gained him, and so falls lower still than the beasts themselves. That would be a sad necessity to have to concede that this distinguishing and nearly boundless faculty is the source of all man's misfortunes; that it is what, slowly, draws him out of that original condition in which his days would slip by in peace and innocence; that it is what, over the course of centuries, produces his discoveries and his mistakes, his virtues and his vices, and in the long run makes him a tyrant over himself and nature alike. It would be dreadful to have to praise as a benefactor whoever first thought of the boards the Orinoco Indians bind onto their children's temples, which preserve for them at least part of their natural simplicity and happiness.

Savage man, left by nature to pure instinct, or rather compensated for what she may have denied him by faculties able to make up for it at once and to raise him afterward far higher, would thus begin with purely animal functions. To see and to feel would be his first condition, shared with every other animal. To want and not to want, to wish and to dread, would be the first and in a way the only workings of his soul, until fresh circumstances caused new developments.

Whatever moralists may say, human understanding owes a great deal to the passions, which in their turn, as everyone agrees, owe a great deal to human understanding. Our reason improves through the activity of our passions; we seek knowledge only because we seek enjoyment, and it is impossible to see why a man free of fears and desires would bother to reason. The passions, for their part, arise from our needs and grow with our progress in knowledge, for we can desire or fear something only because of the ideas we hold of it, or from the plain impulses of nature. Savage man, lacking every kind of knowledge, feels only passions of this last kind. His wishes never extend past his bodily needs. The sole goods he knows are food, a female and rest; the only evils he dreads are pain and hunger. I mean pain, and not death, for no animal as such will ever know what it is to die, and awareness of death and its terrors is among the first things man acquired when he departed from the animal state.

If it were necessary, I could easily cite facts to support this view and show that everywhere the progress of the mind has kept exact pace with the needs that nature left people exposed to, or that circumstances imposed on them, and therefore with the passions that drove them to meet those needs. I could show the arts springing up in Egypt and spreading with the flooding of the Nile. I could follow them among the Greeks, where they were seen to sprout, grow and soar among the sands and rocks of Attica without being able to take root on the fertile banks of the Eurotas. I would point out that, in general, northern peoples are more industrious than southern ones because they can less afford to be otherwise, as if nature meant to even things out by giving their minds the fertility she denied their soil.

But setting aside the uncertain testimony of history, who cannot see that all things seem to take away from savage man all temptation and the ability to change his condition? His imagination paints no pictures for him; his heart asks nothing of him. His modest needs are so easily met by what he finds everywhere at hand, and he is so far from the level of knowledge needed to desire more, that he can possess neither foresight nor curiosity. The spectacle of nature, by becoming wholly familiar to him, finally becomes a matter of equal indifference. It is always the same order, always the same cycles. He lacks the wit to be amazed at the greatest wonders, and it is not in his mind that we should look for the philosophy that a man needs in order to notice for once what he has seen every day. His soul, which nothing disturbs, abandons itself entirely to the sense of its present existence, with no thought of even the nearest future, and his plans, as limited as his outlook, hardly stretch to the end of the day. Such, even now, is the foresight of the Carib: he sells his cotton bed in the morning and comes in the evening, in tears, to buy it back, having failed to foresee that he would need it again the next night.

The longer we think about this matter, the wider the gap between mere sensation and the simplest knowledge appears, and it is impossible to see how man, by his own powers alone, without the help of communication and the goad of necessity, could have crossed so wide a distance. How many centuries may have passed before men saw any fire but that of the heavens? How many different accidents must have combined to teach them the most ordinary uses of this element? How often did they let it die out before they learned to make it again? And how often, perhaps, did each of these secrets perish with its discoverer? What should we say of farming, an art that demands so much labor and foresight, that depends on other arts, and that obviously cannot be practiced except in a society, if not one fully formed then at least one of some standing? Its purpose is not so much to draw food from the earth, since the earth would yield food without all that effort, as to force her to produce the things we like best in preference to others. But let us suppose that men had multiplied so far that the earth's natural yield no longer sufficed to feed them, a supposition which, incidentally, would prove that this way of life was very advantageous to mankind. Let us suppose that, without forge or anvil, farming tools had fallen from heaven into savages' hands; that these men had overcome the deadly dislike they all have of steady work; that they had learned to anticipate their needs so far ahead; that they had worked out how to break the ground, sow seed in it and plant trees; that they had discovered how to grind grain and ferment the juice of grapes. We would have to say they learned all these operations from the gods, since we cannot imagine how they could possibly have found them out unaided. After all these fine gifts, what man would be mad enough to cultivate a field that could be plundered by the first person or animal that took a fancy to its crop? And would anyone agree to spend his days in toil and weariness when the rewards of that toil became more uncertain in proportion to his need of them? In a word, how could this situation persuade men to cultivate the earth as long as it was not divided up among them, that is, as long as the state of nature lasted?

Even if we supposed savage man as skilled in the art of thinking as philosophers make him, even if we made him, as they do, a philosopher himself, discovering the loftiest truths on his own and forming for himself, by the most abstract arguments, maxims of justice and reason drawn from the love of order in general or from the known will of his Creator; in a word, even if we supposed his mind as intelligent and enlightened as it is in fact found to be dull and stupid, what benefit would the species receive from all these metaphysical discoveries, which could not be shared and would die with the individual who made them? What progress could mankind make in the forests, scattered here and there among the other animals? And to what extent could men better and enlighten one another when they had no fixed home and no need of each other's help, when the same people hardly met twice in their lives and, on meeting, neither spoke to nor even recognized one another?

Consider how many ideas we owe to the use of speech, how much grammar trains the mind and makes its operations easier, and reflect, too, on the immense trouble and time the earliest invention of languages must have required. Add these reflections to the previous ones, and we can judge how many thousands of centuries must have been needed to develop, one after another, the operations of which the human mind is capable.

I must now ask permission to pause for a moment to consider the puzzles surrounding the origin of languages. I could simply cite or repeat the inquiries the Abbé de Condillac made into this question, which all fully confirm my system and perhaps even gave me the first idea of it. But the manner in which this philosopher resolves the difficulties he raises himself about the origin of arbitrary signs shows that he assumes what I doubt, namely that some kind of society was already established among the inventors of language. So while I refer to his reflections, I think it my duty to give my own, in order to set out the same difficulties in a light fitted to my subject. The first to appear is how languages could have become necessary. Since men had no dealings with one another and no need for any, we cannot conceive either the need for this invention or its possibility, if it was not indispensable. I might say, like many others, that languages are the fruit of domestic life among fathers, mothers and children. But this would not answer any of the difficulties, and it would commit the same fault as those who, in reasoning about the state of nature, carry into it ideas gathered in society, always imagine families living together under one roof, and suppose their members to keep up between themselves a bond as close and durable as the one we see in a civil state, where so many common interests work to bind them together. In that primitive state, by contrast, there were no houses or huts and no kind of property, and everyone took up lodging at random and seldom stayed more than one night in the same place. Males and females came together by chance, as occasion or desire brought them, without any plan, and they had no great need of language to tell each other their thoughts. They parted just as easily. The mother suckled her children at the start for her own sake, but later, once habit had made them precious to her, out of love for them. The moment they were strong enough to run about looking for food, they left even her of their own accord. Since they had scarcely any means of not losing one another except by staying constantly in each other's sight, they soon reached such a state of forgetfulness that they no longer even recognized one another when they met again. I must also point out that the child, with all his needs to make known and hence more to tell his mother than she has to say to him, is the one who must bear the main cost of invention, and the language he uses must be largely his own work. This makes the number of languages equal to the number of individuals who speak them, and the multiplicity is further increased by their wandering, vagabond way of life, which gives no idiom time to settle into any consistency. To say that the mother would have dictated to the child the words he must use to ask her for this thing or that may well explain how languages already formed are taught, but it does not show us how they are first formed.

Let us suppose this first difficulty overcome. Let us for a moment place ourselves on this side of the immense space that must have separated the pure state of nature from the one in which languages became necessary, and, granting that necessity, ask how languages could begin to be established. This is a new difficulty, still more stubborn than the first. For if men needed speech in order to learn to think, they needed the art of thinking even more to invent the art of speaking. Moreover, even supposing we could picture how vocal sounds came to be taken as the agreed interpreters of our ideas, we would be no closer to knowing who the interpreters of this agreement could have been for ideas that, having no sensible objects, could not be shown by gesture or voice. So we can scarcely frame any acceptable guesses about the birth of this art of communicating our thoughts and setting up a correspondence between minds. It is a sublime art, which, although so close to its origin, philosophers still see at such a prodigious distance from perfection that I have never met one bold enough to say it would ever reach it, even if the revolutions that time unavoidably brings were paused in its favor, even if prejudice could be banished from our academies or would at least consent to keep silent in their presence, and even if these societies devoted themselves entirely, for whole ages, to the study of this knotty subject.

The first language of man, the most universal and most forceful of all languages, in short the only one he needed before it became necessary to persuade assembled crowds, was the cry of nature. Since this cry was drawn from him only by a kind of instinct in the most urgent cases, to beg for help in great danger or relief in great suffering, it was of little use in ordinary life, where gentler feelings generally prevail. When people's ideas started to grow and multiply, and closer contact began to be established among them, they worked to devise more numerous signs and a richer language. They multiplied the tones of the voice and joined gestures to them, which are by nature more expressive and whose meaning depends less on prior agreement. So they expressed visible and moving objects by gestures, and things that strike the ear by imitative sounds. But gestures indicate hardly anything except objects that are present or easily described, and visible actions; they are not universally usable, since darkness or an opaque obstacle makes them useless; and besides, they demand attention rather than attract it. So men finally thought of replacing them with articulations of the voice, which, though they have no similar relation to any particular object, are better suited, as conventional signs, to represent all our ideas. Such a substitution could only have been made by common consent, and in a way that must have been quite hard to carry out for men whose crude organs were untrained by practice. In itself it is still harder to imagine, since the motives for this unanimous agreement must somehow have been expressed, and speech thus seems to have been very necessary in order to establish the use of speech.

We must admit that the words first used by men carried a much broader meaning in their minds than those used in languages of long standing, and that, since they were ignorant of how speech divides into its component parts, they at first gave each word the meaning of an entire sentence. When they later began to notice the difference between subject and attribute and between verb and noun, a distinction that took no small effort of genius, nouns for a time were only so many proper names, the infinitive was the only tense, and as for adjectives, great difficulties must have attended the development of the idea they represent, since every adjective is an abstract word, and abstraction is an unnatural and very painful operation.

At first they gave every object its own name, paying no attention to genus or species, which these first creators of language were in no position to distinguish, and each individual presented itself alone to their minds, just as it stands in the table of nature. If they called one oak A, they called another oak B, so that their vocabulary must have been larger the more limited their knowledge of things was. Getting rid of so sprawling and cumbersome a system of names could not but be very difficult. To arrange the various beings under common, general headings, they would first have had to know their properties and differences, and to be equipped with observations and definitions, that is, to understand natural history and metaphysics, advantages the men of those times could not have had.

Besides, general ideas cannot be conveyed to the mind without words, nor can the understanding grasp them without sentences. This is one reason why mere animals can neither form such ideas nor ever gain the perfectibility that depends on that operation. When a monkey passes from one nut to another without the slightest hesitation, are we to think he has a general idea of that sort of fruit and compares these two particular nuts with an archetype of them in his mind? Certainly not. The sight of one nut calls back to his memory the impressions he got from the other, and his eyes, affected in a certain way, warn his palate of the sensation it is about to have. Every general idea is purely intellectual; let the imagination meddle with it ever so slightly, and it at once becomes a particular idea. Try to picture a tree in general, and you will never manage it. In spite of all your efforts it will come out big or small, sparse or leafy, pale or dark; and if you could make yourself see in it only what is common to all trees, the picture would no longer look like any tree whatsoever. Purely abstract beings are grasped in the same manner, or can be conceived only with the help of speech. Only the definition of a triangle gives you a genuine idea of that figure. As soon as you form a triangle in your mind, it is this or that particular triangle and no other, and you cannot avoid giving its lines thickness and its area color. We must therefore use sentences, and so we must speak, in order to have general ideas; for the moment imagination stops, the mind stops too, unless speech supports it. If, then, the first inventors could only name ideas they already possessed, it follows that the first nouns could never have been anything but proper names.

But when, by means I cannot conceive, our new grammarians began to extend their ideas and make their words general, the inventors' ignorance must have kept this method within very narrow limits. Since at first they had multiplied the names of individuals too much, for lack of knowing the distinctions called genus and species, they later made too few genera and species, for lack of having considered beings in all their differences. To carry the divisions far enough they would have needed more knowledge and experience than we can grant them, and more research and trouble than we can suppose them willing to take. Now if even today we discover new species every day that had escaped all our observation, how many must have escaped the notice of men who judged things only by their first appearance! As for the primary categories and the most general notions, it would be pointless to add that they must have overlooked these too. How, for example, could they have thought of or understood the words matter, spirit, substance, mode, figure and motion, when our own philosophers, who have been using these terms constantly for so long, can barely understand them themselves, and when the ideas attached to these words are purely metaphysical and no models of them could be found in nature?

I stop at these first steps, and I beg my judges to pause their reading a moment and consider how far language still has to go, even in the invention of physical nouns alone, though they are the easiest part of language to invent, before it can express all of man's feelings, take a fixed form, bear being spoken in public and influence society. I earnestly ask them to consider how much time and knowledge must have been needed to find numbers, abstract words, the aorists and all the other tenses of verbs, particles, syntax, the way of linking sentences and arguments and of building up the whole logic of discourse. For my part, I am so alarmed by the difficulties that multiply at every step, and so convinced of the almost demonstrated impossibility that languages could have arisen and been established by purely human means, that I hand over to anyone who cares to take up the examination of this hard problem: "Which was more necessary, a society already formed to invent languages, or languages already invented to form a society?"

But however mysterious the origin of these things may be, we can at least infer, from how little care nature took to bring men together through mutual needs and to make the use of speech easy for them, how little she did to make them sociable, and how little she contributed to anything they themselves have done to become so. In fact, it is impossible to see why, in this primitive state, one man should need another's help any more than one monkey or one wolf needs another of its kind; or, supposing he did, what could induce the other to help him; or even, in that case, how the one who wanted help and the one who was asked could agree on terms. Authors, I know, keep telling us that in this state man would have been a most miserable creature. If it is true, as I believe I have shown, that he must have continued for many ages without either the desire or the opportunity to leave that state, this claim could only serve to indict nature, not the being nature made so. But if I properly grasp the word "miserable," it either has no sense or signifies nothing but a painful deprivation and a suffering state of body or soul. Now I would like to know what kind of misery could belong to a free being whose heart is perfectly at peace and whose body is perfectly healthy. And which is likelier to become intolerable to those who live it, civil life or natural life? In civil life we can hardly meet a single person who does not complain of his existence; many even throw away as much of it as they can, and the combined force of divine and human laws can scarcely curb this disorder. Was any free savage ever known to be so much as tempted to complain of life and lay violent hands on himself? Let us judge, then, with less pride, on which side real misery lies. On the contrary, nothing could be more wretched than savage man dazzled by flashes of knowledge, tormented by passions, and reasoning about a condition different from the one he found himself in.
