It was by a very wise providence that the faculties he held in potential were meant to develop only as occasions arose to exercise them, lest they be superfluous or burdensome to him before he needed them, or slow and useless when he did. In his instinct alone he had everything he needed to live in a state of nature; in his cultivated reason he has barely what he needs to live in society.

It seems at first sight that, since there was no kind of moral relation among men in this state, nor any known duties, they could be neither good nor bad and had neither vices nor virtues, unless we take these words in a physical sense and call vices, in the individual, the qualities that may harm his own survival, and virtues those that may help it. In that case we would have to consider as most virtuous the man who put up the least resistance to the simple impulses of nature. But without departing from the usual meaning of these terms, it is right to suspend the judgment we might form about such a situation and to guard against prejudice, until we have weighed up, scales in hand, whether there are more virtues or vices among civilized men. We should also ask whether the improvement of their understanding is enough to make up for the harm they do each other as they become better informed about the services they ought to render, or whether, on the whole, they would not be much happier in a condition where they had nothing to fear or hope for from each other than in the one where they have submitted to universal dependence and bound themselves to rely for everything on the goodwill of those who do not consider themselves obliged to give anything in return.

But above all, let us beware of concluding with Hobbes that man, having no concept of goodness, must be inherently bad; that he is vicious because he does not know what virtue is; that he always refuses to do any service for his fellows because he believes none is owed; and that, because of the right he justly claims to everything he needs, he foolishly regards himself as the owner of the whole universe. Hobbes saw very clearly the flaws in all the modern definitions of natural right, yet the conclusions he draws from his own definition show that, in the sense he understands it, it is just as open to objection. To argue from his own principles, this author should have said that the state of nature, as the state in which concern for our own survival interferes least with the survival of others, was by that very fact the most favorable to peace and the best suited to mankind. He says the very opposite because he rashly included, among the objects of the care savage man should take for his survival, the satisfaction of countless passions that are society's creation and have made laws necessary. According to him, "a bad man is a sturdy child." But this does not prove that savage man is a sturdy child; and even if we conceded that he was, what could this philosopher infer from it? That if this man, when robust, depended on others as much as when feeble, there is no excess he would not commit. He would not hesitate to hit his mother if she was slow giving him the breast; he would claw, bite and strangle without remorse the first of his younger brothers who happened to jostle or annoy him. But these are two contradictory suppositions in the state of nature: to be robust and to be dependent. Man is weak when dependent, and is his own master until he grows robust. Hobbes did not see that the same cause that keeps savages from using their reason, as our jurists claim, also keeps them from misusing their faculties, as he himself claims. So we can say that savages are not bad precisely because they have no idea what being good means; for it is neither the growth of understanding nor the restraint of law, but the calm of their passions and their ignorance of vice, that stops them from doing ill: tanto plus in illis proficit Vitiorum ignorantia, quam in his cognitio Virtutis. There is also another principle that Hobbes missed. It was given to man to moderate, on certain occasions, the blind and impetuous outbursts of self-love, or the desire for self-preservation that existed before that passion appeared, and it tempers the ardor with which he naturally pursues his own welfare through an innate repugnance at seeing beings like himself suffer. I will surely not be contradicted if I grant man the one natural virtue that even the most passionate detractor of human virtues could not deny him, I mean pity, a disposition suited to creatures as weak as we are and exposed to so many ills. It is a virtue all the more universal and useful to man because it precedes every form of reflection, and so natural that the beasts themselves sometimes show clear signs of it. Not to speak of the tenderness of mothers toward their young and the dangers they face to shield them from danger, consider how reluctant horses are to trample living bodies. One animal never passes the corpse of another of its kind without being disturbed; there are even some that give their dead companions a kind of burial; and the sorrowful bellowing of cattle entering the slaughterhouse reveals the impression the horrible sight there makes on them. It is a pleasure to see the author of the Fable of the Bees forced to acknowledge man as a compassionate and sensitive being, and, in the example he gives to prove it, setting aside his cold, subtle style to put before us the moving picture of a man who, with his hands tied, is forced to watch a wild beast tear a child from its mother's arms, crush the tender limbs with its teeth, and rip the throbbing entrails of the innocent victim with its claws. What horrible emotions must such a spectator feel at an event that does not concern him personally? What anguish must he suffer at being unable to help the fainting mother or the dying infant?

Such is the pure impulse of nature, prior to any kind of reflection; such is the force of natural pity, which the most dissolute morals have so far found hard to extinguish. We see every day in our theaters that men sympathize with the unfortunate and weep at their sufferings who, in the tyrant's place, would only make their enemies' torments worse. Mandeville clearly saw that, for all their moral codes, men would never have been anything but monsters if nature had not given them pity to assist reason. But he failed to see that from this quality alone come all the social virtues he wishes to deny mankind. What are generosity, mercy and humanity, in fact, but pity applied to the weak, to the guilty, or to the human species in general? Even benevolence and friendship, rightly understood, turn out to be the effects of a constant pity fixed on a particular object; for to wish that someone not suffer, what is that but to wish him happy? Even granting it were the case that compassion is merely a sentiment that puts us in the sufferer's place, a feeling dim but active in the savage, developed but dormant in civilized man, how could that idea affect the truth of what I say, except to make it plainer? Compassion must in fact be all the stronger the more intimately the animal that witnesses the distress identifies itself with the animal that suffers it. Now it is evident that this identification must have been infinitely closer in the state of nature than in the state of reason. It is reason that engenders self-love and reflection that strengthens it. Reason turns man in on himself; reason makes him keep away from anything that might trouble or afflict him. Philosophy isolates him; it is through her teaching that he mutters, at the sight of another in distress, "Perish if you like, I am safe." Nothing less than evils threatening the whole species can disturb the philosopher's quiet sleep and drag him from his bed. A man can be murdered beneath his window with impunity; the philosopher needs only to clap his hands over his ears and argue with himself a little to keep nature, which rebels within him, from identifying him with the victim. Savage man lacks this admirable talent; for want of wisdom and reason he always rushes foolishly to obey the first whisper of humanity. In riots and street brawls the crowd gathers while the prudent man slips away. It is the rabble, the market women, who separate the combatants and stop gentlemen from cutting each other's throats.

It is certain, then, that pity is a natural feeling which, by tempering in each individual the activity of self-love, contributes to the mutual preservation of the whole species. It is pity that carries us without reflection to the aid of those we see suffering. In the state of nature it stands in for laws, morals and virtue, with the added advantage that nobody is tempted to disobey its soft voice. It is pity that will always keep a robust savage from robbing a feeble child or a frail old man of the food they have gained with effort and hardship, so long as he has any hope of finding his own by other means. It is pity that, in place of that lofty maxim of reasoned justice, "Do to others what you would wish others to do to you," inspires all men with that other maxim of natural goodness, far less perfect but perhaps more useful: "Pursue your own good with as little harm to others as you can." In short, not in subtle arguments but in this natural feeling is where we must search for the cause of the reluctance every man would feel to do evil, even apart from the lessons of education. It may be the particular good fortune of Socrates and other minds of his kind to reason themselves into virtue, but the human race would long ago have died out if its survival had depended entirely on the reasoning of the individuals who make it up.

With passions so mild and so healthy a restraint, men who were more wild than wicked, and more concerned to protect themselves from harm than to inflict it on other animals, were not exposed to dangerous quarrels. They had no dealings with one another, and so knew nothing of vanity, respect, esteem or contempt. They had no notion of what we call mine and yours, and no true idea of justice. They regarded any violence done to them as an injury easily made good, not as an offense deserving punishment, and they never so much as dreamed of revenge, except perhaps mechanically and on the spur of the moment, like a dog that bites the stone thrown at it. Their disputes would seldom have ended in bloodshed if they had never been caused by anything more serious than food. But there is a more dangerous cause of conflict, which I must not leave unmentioned.

Of the many passions that move the human heart there is one of a hot and impetuous nature which makes the two sexes necessary to each other, a terrible passion that scorns every danger, sweeps aside every obstacle, and in its frenzy seems fit to destroy the very human race it is meant to preserve. What would become of men given over to this lawless and brutal rage, without modesty and without shame, fighting every day over the objects of their desire at the cost of their blood?

We must first admit that the fiercer the passions, the more necessary laws are to restrain them. But apart from the disorders and crimes these passions cause among us every day, which sufficiently prove that laws are not enough for the purpose, we would do well to look back a little further and ask whether these evils did not arise together with the laws themselves. On that view, even if laws were capable of repressing these evils, it would be the least we could expect of them, since it would be no more than stopping the spread of a harm they themselves had produced.

Let us begin by distinguishing what is moral from what is physical in the passion called love. The physical part is that general desire which impels the sexes to come together; the moral part is what directs this desire and fixes it on one particular object to the exclusion of all others, or at least gives it greater intensity toward its preferred object. It is not hard to see that the moral side of love is a manufactured feeling, arising from society and carefully and skillfully promoted by women in order to establish their rule and give the sex that ought to obey the power to command. This feeling rests on certain notions of beauty and merit that a savage cannot have, and on comparisons that he cannot make, so it can hardly exist in him. His mind was never able to form abstract ideas of regularity and proportion, and neither is his heart open to feelings of admiration and love, which, without our noticing it, arise from applying those ideas. He listens only to the instincts nature planted in him, not to a taste he never had the means to acquire, and any woman will serve his purpose.

Limited entirely to the physical side of love, and fortunate enough not to know the preferences that sharpen the appetite while making it harder to satisfy, men in the state of nature must be subject to fewer and less violent fits of this passion, and consequently to fewer and less violent quarrels because of it. Imagination, which causes so much havoc among us, never speaks to the hearts of savages. They calmly wait for nature's promptings and yield to them without choosing, with more pleasure than fury, and their desires do not outlast their need of the thing desired.

Nothing, then, is plainer than that it is society alone that has added to love, as to all the other passions, the impetuous ardor that so often makes it fatal to mankind. It is all the more ridiculous to portray savages as constantly murdering each other to satisfy their brutality, since this view directly contradicts experience. The Caribs, who of all people in the world have so far departed least from the state of nature, are in reality the most peaceful in their love affairs and the least subject to jealousy, although they live in a burning climate that seems always to add considerably to the intensity of these passions.

As for the conclusions that may be drawn, for various animal species, from the fights of the males, who at all seasons cover our poultry yards with blood and in spring make our forests echo with the noise of their struggles over females, we must begin by excluding every species in which nature has plainly established relations between the sexes' strength that differ from those among us. So from the fights of cocks we can draw no conclusion that touches the human species. In the species where the proportion is better kept, these fights must be due wholly to the shortage of females relative to males, or, what amounts to the same, to the intervals during which the females constantly refuse the males' advances. For if the female admits the male for only two months a year, it is just as if the number of females were five sixths smaller than it is. Neither case applies to the human species, where the females generally outnumber the males, and where nobody has ever observed, even among savages, that females have, like those of other animals, set seasons of passion and indifference. Besides, in several of these animals the whole species catches fire at once, and for some days there is nothing to be seen but confusion, uproar, disorder and bloodshed, a state unknown in the human species, where love is never periodical. So we cannot conclude from the fights of certain animals over their females that the same would happen to man in the state of nature. Besides, even supposing we could, since these contests do not destroy the other species, there is at least equal reason to think they would not be fatal to ours. Indeed it is very likely they would cause less havoc than they do in society, especially in those countries where, morality still being held in some esteem, lovers' jealousy and husbands' vengeance produce duels, murders and even worse crimes every day; where the duty of eternal fidelity serves only to breed adultery; and where the very laws of chastity and honor necessarily help to increase dissoluteness and multiply abortions.

Let us conclude that savage man, wandering in the forests without industry, without speech, without a fixed home, a stranger alike to war and to every social tie, with no need of his fellows and no desire to harm them, perhaps without even telling them apart as individuals, subject to few passions and finding in himself all he needs, had no knowledge or feelings except those that suit that condition. He sensed only his real needs, noticed only what it was in his interest to see, and his understanding made as little progress as his vanity. If he happened to make some discovery, he could the less pass it on because he did not even know his own children. The art died with its inventor; there was no education and no improvement; generations followed generations to no purpose; and since each started from the same point, whole centuries passed in the crudeness and barbarity of the first age. The species had grown old while the individual remained in a state of childhood.

If I have dwelt so long on this supposed primitive condition, it is because I felt it my duty, given how many ancient errors and deep-rooted prejudices I have to uproot, to dig down to the very roots and to show, with a true portrait of the state of nature, to what degree even natural inequality falls short, in that state, of the reality and influence our writers ascribe to it.

In fact, it is easy to see that among the differences that distinguish men, several pass for natural that are merely the work of habit and of the various ways of life that men take up in society. Thus a sturdy or fragile constitution, and the strength or weakness that goes with it, more often come from the hardy or soft way a man was brought up than from the original build of his body. The same is true of mental powers. Education not only creates a difference between minds that are cultivated and minds that are not, it even widens the difference among the cultivated ones in proportion to their training; for if a giant and a dwarf set out on the same road, the giant gains a new advantage over the dwarf at every step. Now compare the enormous variety in the schooling and lifestyle of the different classes in a civil state with the simplicity and uniformity of animal and savage life, where every individual eats the same food, lives the same way and does exactly the same things. We can easily see how much smaller the gap between one man and another must be in the state of nature than in the state of society, and how much every inequality of institution must increase the natural inequalities of the human race.

But even if nature, in handing out her gifts, really did show all the preferences ascribed to her, what advantage could the most favored gain from her partiality, at the expense of others, in a state of affairs that hardly allowed any relations between her pupils? What use is beauty where there is no love? What good is wit to people who do not talk, or cleverness to those who have no affairs to transact? Authors keep crying out that the strongest would oppress the weakest; but let them explain what they mean by the word oppression. One man will rule with violence, another will groan under constant subjection to his every whim. That is exactly what I observe among us, but I cannot see how it can be said of savage men, into whose heads it would be hard even to drive the meaning of the words domination and servitude. One man might indeed take the fruits another had collected, the game another had killed, the cave another had taken for shelter; but how could he ever demand obedience from him, and what chains of dependence can there be among men who own nothing? If I am driven from one tree, I only have to look for another; if one place is made unpleasant for me, what can stop me from settling elsewhere? But suppose I met a man so much stronger than me, and at the same time so wicked, so lazy and so savage, as to force me to provide for his food while he stays idle. He would have to resolve never to look away from me for even a moment, and to tie me up securely before he could take the briefest nap, for fear that I would kill him or escape while he slept. That is to say, he would have to expose himself willingly to far greater trouble than the trouble he wants to avoid, or any he causes me. And in the end, let him relax his vigilance ever so little, let him turn his head the other way at some sudden noise, and I am already lost in the forest, my fetters are broken, and he never sees me again.

But without insisting any longer on these details, anyone can see that since the ties of servitude are made only by men's mutual dependence on each other and by the reciprocal needs that bind them together, it is impossible to enslave a man without first putting him in a position where he cannot live without the enslaver's help. That position does not exist in a state of nature, which leaves every man his own master and makes the law of the strongest wholly vain and useless.

Having proved that the inequality that can exist between man and man in a state of nature is almost imperceptible and has very little influence, I must now go on to show its origin and follow its progress through the successive stages of the human mind's growth. I have shown that perfectibility, the social virtues and the remaining faculties that natural man had received only in potential could never develop by themselves; that for this a chance combination of several outside causes was needed, which might never happen, and without which he would have stayed forever in his primitive state. I must now consider and bring together the various accidents that may have perfected the human understanding by debasing the species, made a being wicked by making him sociable, and from so distant a starting point brought man and the world at last to the point where we now see them.

I must admit that, since the events I am about to describe might have happened in many different ways, my choice of those I will present can rest on nothing but conjecture. But conjectures become reasons when they are not only the most probable that can be drawn from the nature of things but the only means we have of discovering the truth. And the consequences I mean to draw from mine will not be merely conjectural, since on the principles I have just established it is impossible to form any other system that would not give me the same results and allow me to draw the same conclusions.

This entitles me to be briefer in my reflections on the way the passage of time makes up for the improbability of events; on the surprising power of very trivial causes when they act without interruption; on the impossibility, in one direction, of refuting certain hypotheses if, on the other, we cannot give them the degree of certainty that facts must be allowed to have; on the fact that when two facts are put forward as real, it is the business of history to link them by a chain of intermediate facts that are unknown or taken to be so, and to supply the facts that actually connect them, and the business of philosophy, when history is silent, to point out similar facts that can serve the same purpose; and finally on the privilege of resemblance, in regard to events, to reduce facts to a much smaller number of distinct classes than is commonly supposed. It suffices me to present these matters to my judges for their consideration; it is enough for me to have conducted my inquiry in such a way as to spare ordinary readers the trouble of considering them.

chapters.title: Second Part
paragraphs: The first man who fenced off a piece of ground and took it into his head to say "This is mine," and found people simple enough to believe him, was the true founder of civil society. What crimes, wars and killings, what miseries and horrors, would the human race have been spared by the one who yanked out the stakes or levelled the ditch and cried out to his fellows: "Do not listen to this impostor. You are lost if you forget that the earth's fruits belong to all of us and the land itself to nobody!" Now it is quite probable that matters had by now reached a point where they could not go on much longer as they were. For the notion of property rests on several earlier ideas that could only arise gradually, one after another, and it was not formed all at once in the human mind. Men must have made great progress, gained a large store of skill and knowledge, and passed it on and added to it from age to age, before they reached this final point in the state of nature. Let us therefore take up matters from a little earlier and gather into a single view, in their most natural order, this slow succession of events and mental advances.

The first thing man felt was his own existence, and his first concern was to preserve it. The produce of the earth gave him all the help he needed, and instinct led him to use it. Among the various appetites that made him experience different modes of existence at different times, there was one that urged him to perpetuate his species. This blind inclination, quite without anything like true love or affection, produced only a purely animal act. Once the immediate heat was spent, the sexes took no further notice of each other, and even the child had no tie to its mother as soon as it no longer needed her help.

Such was the condition of infant man, such was the life of an animal confined at first to pure sensations, and so far from thinking of forcing nature's gifts from her that he hardly made use even of those she offered him freely. But difficulties soon arose, and he had to learn how to overcome them. The height of some trees, which kept him from reaching their fruit; the competition of other animals just as fond of the same fruit; the ferocity of many that threatened his very life: all these circumstances forced him to train his body. He had to become active, fleet of foot and tough in a fight. The natural weapons, stones and tree branches, soon came to his hand. He learned to get past nature's obstacles, to battle other animals when necessary, to contest his food even against other men, or to compensate for whatever he had to give up to the strongest.

As the human race grew more numerous and spread out, its hardships multiplied and grew too. Differences of soil, climate and season may have forced men to adopt different ways of living. Bad harvests, long hard winters and scorching summers that dried up all the fruits of the earth demanded extraordinary efforts of ingenuity. On seacoasts and riverbanks they invented the fishing line and the hook and became fishermen and fish-eaters. In the woods they fashioned bows and arrows and turned into hunters and warriors. In cold lands they covered themselves with the skins of the beasts they had killed. Thunder, a volcano or some lucky accident introduced them to fire, a new defense against the rigors of winter. They found out how to keep this element alive, then how to produce it again, and finally how to use it to prepare the flesh of animals, which they had until then devoured raw from the carcass.

This repeated application of different beings to himself and to one another must naturally have produced in man's mind the idea of certain relations. These relations, which we express by the words great, small, strong, weak, fast, slow, timid, bold and the like, were compared from time to time, almost without his thinking about it. They produced in him a sort of reflection, or rather a mechanical caution, which pointed out the precautions most essential to his survival and safety.

The new insights that came from this development increased his superiority over other animals by making him aware of it. He set himself to trap them and played them a thousand tricks. Though several surpassed him in strength or speed, in time he became master of those that could be of use to him and a dangerous enemy to those that could harm him. Thus his first look into himself produced his first stirring of pride. Thus, at a time when he could scarcely tell the different ranks of existence apart, by giving his species first rank among animals in general he prepared himself from afar to claim it as an individual among his own kind in particular.

Although other men were not to him what they are to us, and he had hardly more contact with them than with other animals, they were not overlooked in his observations. The similarities he might in time discover among them, and between them and his mate, led him to judge about those he could not see. Noticing that they all acted as he would have done in similar circumstances, he concluded that their way of thinking and wanting was entirely like his own. Once this important truth was engraved deeply on his mind, it made him follow, by a presentiment as sure as any logic and much quicker, the best rules of conduct that it was wise for his own safety and advantage to observe toward them.

Taught by experience that the love of happiness is the sole principle of all human actions, he found himself able to pick out the few cases in which shared interest might justify counting on the help of his fellows, and the even fewer in which a clash of interests might rightly make it suspect. In the first case he joined with them in one herd, or at most in some sort of free association that bound none of its members and lasted no longer than the passing need that had produced it. In the second case, each pursued his own advantage, either by open force if he felt strong enough, or by cunning and skill if he thought himself too weak to use violence.

This is how men may have gradually acquired some crude idea of their mutual commitments and of the advantage of keeping them, but only so far as their immediate and tangible interest required. Foresight was entirely foreign to them, and far from worrying about the distant future, they hardly thought of the next day. If a deer was to be caught, everyone saw that to succeed he must faithfully hold his post. But if a hare chanced to run past within reach of one of them, we may be sure he chased it without scruple, and having caught his prey never reproached himself for making his companions miss theirs.

We can easily imagine that such dealings hardly required a more refined language than that of crows or monkeys, which flock together in much the same way. Inarticulate cries, many gestures and some imitative sounds must have been the universal language of mankind for a long time. By adding to these, in each country, some articulate and conventional sounds, whose establishment, as I have already hinted, is not very easy to explain, particular languages arose, though rough and imperfect ones, much like those still found today among several savage nations. My pen, hemmed in by the hurry of time, by the wealth of what I have to say, and by the barely noticeable progress of the first improvements, flies like an arrow over countless ages; for the slower the succession of events, the faster I may allow myself to be in reporting them.

At length these first advances enabled man to advance faster. Skill grew more perfect as the mind became more enlightened. Men soon ceased dropping off to sleep beneath the first tree or taking shelter in the first cave. They came across certain hard, sharp kinds of stone that resembled spades or axes and used them to dig the ground, cut down trees, and build huts from the branches, which they later thought of plastering with clay or mud. This was the era of a first revolution, which set up and differentiated families, and brought in a kind of property and with it perhaps a thousand quarrels and fights. Yet since the strongest were likely the first to make huts for themselves that they knew they could defend, we may conclude that the weak found it quicker and safer to copy them than to attempt to drive them out. As for those who already had huts, no one could have had much temptation to seize his neighbor's, not so much because it did not belong to him as because it would be of no use to him, and because, to take possession of it, he would have to expose himself to a very fierce fight with the present occupants.

The first developments of the heart were the result of a new situation that united husbands and wives, parents and children under one roof. The habit of living together gave birth to the sweetest feelings the human species knows, conjugal and parental love. Each family became a small society, all the more firmly united because mutual attachment and freedom were its only bonds. It was then that the sexes, whose manner of living had until now been the same, began to adopt different manners and customs. Women became more settled and grew used to staying at home and looking after the children, while the men roamed abroad in search of food for the whole family. By living a little more comfortably, the two sexes also began to lose some of their usual fierceness and toughness. But if on the one hand individuals became less able to fight wild beasts one by one, on the other they were more easily brought together to resist them in common.

In this new state of affairs, the simplicity and solitude of man's life, the smallness of his wants, and the tools he had devised to meet them gave him plenty of free time, which he used to give himself several comforts unknown to his forebears. This was the first yoke he unknowingly laid on himself and the first source of trouble he prepared for his children. For besides continuing in this way to soften both body and mind, these comforts, having through use lost nearly all their power to please and even turned into genuine needs, made going without them far more unbearable than having them had been pleasant. To lose them was a misfortune, but to possess them was no happiness.

Here we may perceive a bit better how the use of language gradually begins or improves in the heart of each family, and we may also form conjectures about how various particular causes might have spread language and speeded its progress by making it more necessary every day. Great floods or earthquakes surrounded inhabited regions with water or cliffs. Portions of the mainland were torn off by upheavals of the globe and split into islands. It is clear that among men thus brought together and forced to live side by side, a common idiom must have sprung up much sooner than among those who roamed freely through the forests of the mainland. So it is quite possible that the inhabitants of the islands formed in this way, after their first attempts at navigation, brought speech to us; and it is at the very least probable that society and languages began on islands and even reached perfection there before the inhabitants of the continent knew anything of either.

Everything now begins to take on a new look. Those who had until now wandered through the woods, by adopting a more settled way of life, gradually draw together, join into separate groups, and finally form distinct nations in each country, united in character and customs not by any laws or regulations but by a uniform way of life, the same foods and the shared influence of climate. Permanent neighborhood must in the end inevitably create some connection between different families. The passing contacts demanded by nature soon produced, among the young people of both sexes living in neighboring huts, another kind of contact, which besides being equally pleasant is made more lasting by frequent meeting. Men begin to look at different objects and make comparisons; they gradually acquire ideas of merit and beauty, and these soon produce feelings of preference. By seeing each other often they form a habit that makes it painful not to see each other always. Tender and pleasant feelings steal into the soul and are wound up by the slightest opposition into the most violent fury. Jealousy awakens with love; discord triumphs; and the gentlest of passions demands sacrifices of human blood to appease it.

As ideas and feelings follow one another and the head and heart are exercised, men continue to shake off their original wildness, and their relations become closer and wider. They now begin to gather around a great tree. Singing and dancing, the genuine children of love and leisure, become the amusement, or rather the occupation, of idle men and women thus assembled. Each begins to look at the others and to want to be looked at himself, and public esteem acquires a value. The one who sings or dances best, the handsomest, the strongest, the most skillful, the most eloquent, comes to be the most respected. This was the first move toward inequality and, simultaneously moment, toward vice. From these earliest preferences came vanity and contempt on one side and envy and shame on the other; and the fermentation produced by these new leavens eventually produced combinations fatal to happiness and innocence.

No sooner had men begun to value one another and to know what esteem was, each claimed a right to it, and it was no longer safe for anyone to withhold it from another. From this came the first duties of civility and politeness, even among savages; and from this every deliberate injury became an insult, because, besides the harm it caused, the offended party was sure to find in it a contempt for his person that was harder to bear than the harm itself. Thus, since each man punished the contempt shown him in proportion to the value he set on himself, revenge became terrible, and men learned to be bloodthirsty and cruel. Such precisely was the stage reached by most of the savage nations we know. It is because of a failure to distinguish ideas clearly and to notice how far these peoples were from the first state of nature that so many authors have hastily concluded that man is naturally cruel and needs a regular system of policing to be tamed. Nothing is milder than man in his primitive condition, when nature has placed him at an equal distance from the stupidity of brutes and the harmful cleverness of civilized man, and when, held by instinct and reason alike to protecting himself against the harm that threatens him, he is held back by natural compassion from inflicting any injury to others, so far from being in the least inclined to repay even one he has received. For, according to the axiom of the wise Locke, "Where there is no property, there can be no injury."

But we must notice that the society now formed, and the relations now established among men, required qualities different from those they had from their primitive constitution. As a sense of morality began to enter into human actions, and every man, before there were laws, was the only judge and avenger of the wrongs he suffered, the goodness of heart suited to the pure state of nature was by no means suited to infant society. Punishments had to become harsher as opportunities to offend became more frequent, and the fear of vengeance had to add strength to the too weak curb of the law. So even though men had grown less patient and natural compassion had already suffered some change, this stage in the development of human faculties, holding a middle point between the indolence of the primitive state and the restless activity of self-love, must have been the happiest and most lasting period. The more we think about this state, the more convinced we become that it was the least subject to upheaval and the best for man, and that nothing could have drawn him out of it except some fatal accident which, for the common good, should never have happened. The example of the savages, most of whom have been found in this condition, seems to confirm that mankind was made to remain in it forever; that this condition is the real youth of the world; and that all later advances have been so many steps, apparently toward the perfection of the individual, but really fact toward the decline of the species.

As long as men were satisfied with their rustic huts, as long as they limited themselves to clothes of animal skins stitched together with thorns and fishbones, as long as they thought feathers and shells enough for decoration and painted their bodies different colors, as long as they improved or decorated their bows and arrows, carved little fishing boats or clumsy musical instruments out of wood with sharp-edged stones, in a word as long as they undertook only tasks that one person could finish and stuck to arts that did not need the combined efforts of several hands, they lived free, healthy, honest and happy, as far as their nature permitted, and kept enjoying the pleasures of independent dealings with each other. But from the moment one man needed another's help, from the moment it seemed useful for one man to have enough supplies for two, equality vanished, property appeared, work became necessary, and the boundless forests turned into smiling fields that had to be watered with human sweat, and in which slavery and misery were soon seen to spring up and flourish along with the crops.

Metallurgy and agriculture were the two arts whose invention brought about this great revolution. For the poet it is gold and silver, but for the philosopher it is iron and corn that civilized men and ruined mankind. Accordingly neither was known among the savages of America, who for that very reason have always remained savages. Other nations seem to have stayed barbarous as long as they practiced only one of these arts without the other. Perhaps one of the best reasons for why Europe has been, if not earlier, at least more steadily and better civilized than the other parts of the world is that it is both the richest in iron and the best suited to growing corn.

It is very hard to say how men came to know about iron and the art of using it. We should not suppose they could have thought by themselves of digging it out from the mine and readying it for smelting before they knew what such a process would produce. On the other hand, there is even less reason to credit this discovery to some accidental fire, since mines form only in dry and barren places stripped of trees and plants, so that it looks as if nature had gone to trouble to conceal so harmful a secret from us. Nothing remains, then, but the extraordinary circumstance of some volcano that, spewing out molten metal, gave those who watched the idea of imitating nature's operation. Even so, we must suppose them to have had an uncommon stock of courage and foresight to take on so toilsome a job and to see so far ahead the advantages they might gain from it. These are qualities hardly suited to minds more practiced than we can imagine those of such discoverers to have been.

Regarding farming, its principles were understood long before its practice began, and it is hardly possible that men, constantly busy drawing their food from trees and plants, would not early have hit on the means nature uses to produce vegetation. But it was in all probability very late before their industry turned that way. Perhaps trees, which together with land and water game gave them enough food, did not need their attention; or they did not know the use of grain; or they had no tools to cultivate it; or they lacked foresight about future needs; or finally, they had no means of stopping others from carrying off the fruit of their labor. We may suppose that, once they became more industrious, they began farming by growing a few beans or roots around their huts with sharp stones and pointed sticks, and that it was a long time before they learned to prepare grain and had the tools necessary to grow it in quantity. And there is also the need, in order to pursue this occupation and sow fields, to agree to lose something now in order to gain much later, a precaution very foreign to the turn of mind of man in the savage state, in which, as I have already noted, he can hardly foresee his needs from morning to night.

For this reason the invention of other arts must have been necessary to force mankind to take up agriculture. As soon as men were needed to smelt and forge iron, others were needed to feed them. The more hands were employed in manufacturing, the fewer were left to provide food for everyone, though the number of mouths to feed stayed the same. And as some demanded goods in exchange for their iron, the rest at last discovered how to make iron serve to multiply goods. Hence arose, on the one hand, farming and agriculture, and on the other the craft of working metals and increasing their uses.

From the cultivation of the earth, its division necessarily followed, and from property once recognized, the first rules of justice. For in order to secure to every man what is his, every man must have something. Moreover, as men began to look ahead to the future and all found themselves holding more or less goods that could be lost, each had reason to fear reprisals for any wrong he might do to others. This origin is the more natural since we cannot imagine how property could arise from any source other than labor. For what can a man add, in order to acquire property in things he has not made, except his work? It is labor alone that, by giving the farmer a claim to the produce of the land he has tilled, gives him a claim to the land itself, at least until the harvest, and so from year to year; and since this continuous use amounts to uninterrupted possession, it is easily turned into property. The ancients, says Grotius, by giving Ceres the epithet of lawgiver and calling a festival in her honor the Thesmophoria, suggested that the division of lands created a new kind of right, that is, the right of property, different from the one that follows from the law of nature.

Things so arranged might have remained equal if men's talents had been equal, and if, for instance, the use of iron and the consumption of goods had always been in exact proportion to each other. But since nothing supported this balance, it was soon broken. The strongest performed the most labor; the most dexterous made the best use of his work; the most inventive found ways of reducing his labor. The farmer needed more iron, or the smith more corn; and although both worked equally, one earned a great deal by his labor while the other could barely live by his. In this way natural inequality gradually unfolds itself alongside that which arises from various combinations, and the differences among men, developed by differences in their circumstances, become more noticeable and more lasting in their effects, and begin to influence the condition of individuals in the same proportion.

Once matters had reached this point, it is simple to picture the rest. I shall not stop to describe the successive inventions of the other arts, the progress of language, the testing and employment of talents, the inequality of fortunes, the use or abuse of wealth, nor all the details that follow from these and that anyone can easily supply. I will only glance at mankind placed in this new order of things.

Behold, then, all our faculties developed: memory and imagination at work, self-love engaged, reason made active, and the mind almost at the furthest limits of the perfection it is capable of. Behold all our natural qualities set in motion. The rank and condition of every man is now established, not only by the amount of his property and his power to help or harm others, but also by intelligence, beauty, strength or skill, merit or talent. Since these were the only qualities that could win respect, it became necessary to have them or at least to pretend to. Men had to seem to be what they really were not. To be and to appear became two very different things, and from this distinction came ostentation and deceit and all the vices that follow in their train. On the other hand, man, formerly free and independent, was now, through a multitude of new needs, brought into subjection, so to speak, to all of nature and especially to his fellows. He became their slave in a sense even by becoming their master: if rich, he needed their services; if poor, their help; even a middling condition could not let him do without them. He had to keep working, therefore, to get them interested in his welfare and to make them, if not in reality then at least in appearance, find their advantage in laboring for his. This made him sly and devious with some, domineering and harsh with others, and forced him to treat badly all those he needed whenever he could not frighten them into obeying and did not find it in his interest to buy their compliance with real services. In short, an insatiable ambition, a burning desire to increase their relative fortunes, not so much from real need as to rise above others, inspires in all men a wicked inclination to harm each other and a secret jealousy that is all the more dangerous because, to gain its end more safely, it often puts on the face of kindness. In a word, there was on one side competition and rivalry and on the other a clash of interests, while a secret desire to profit at others' expense always prevailed. Such were the first effects of property and the inseparable companions of infant inequality.

Before the invention of signs to represent it, wealth could hardly consist of anything but land and cattle, the only real goods men can possess. But when estates grew so numerous and large as to cover whole countries and touch one another, it became impossible for one man to increase his holdings except at another's expense. The surplus inhabitants, who were too weak or too idle to make such gains in their turn, grew poor without losing anything, because while everything around them changed they alone stayed the same, and they were obliged to receive or seize their living from the hands of the rich. From this began to flow, according to each person's character, domination and slavery, or violence and plunder. The rich for their part had scarcely begun to taste the pleasure of commanding when they preferred it to every other, and using their old slaves to win new ones, they thought only of subjugating and enslaving their neighbors, like ravenous wolves that, having once tasted human flesh, refuse all other food and from then on devour only men.

In this way the most powerful or the most wretched, each regarding their strength or their misery as a kind of claim on other people's property, equivalent even to a right of ownership, brought about, once equality was broken, the most shocking disorders. In this way the usurpations of the rich, the robberies of the poor and the unbridled passions of all, by stifling the cries of natural compassion and the as yet faint voice of justice, made man greedy, wicked and ambitious. Between the right of the strongest and the right of the first occupant there arose a perpetual conflict, which always ended in fighting and bloodshed. Infant society became the scene of the most horrible warfare. Mankind, thus degraded and tormented, no longer able to turn back or to give up the unhappy gains it had made, and working only toward its own ruin through the abuse of faculties that in themselves do it so much honor, brought itself to the very brink of destruction.
Stunned by the strangeness of his plight, rich and yet wretched, he longs to escape the wealth he lately begged for, and hates what he once prayed to have.

But it is impossible that men should not sooner or later have thought about so miserable a situation and about the calamities that engulfed them. The rich in particular must soon have realized how much they suffered from a perpetual war whose whole cost they alone bore, and in which, although everyone risked his life, they alone risked their property. Besides, whatever color they tried to give their usurpations, they saw well enough that these were basically founded on false and shaky claims, and that what they had acquired by mere force others could take back from them by mere force, without giving them the least ground for complaint. Even those who owed all their wealth to their own industry could hardly rest their holdings on a better claim. It did them no good to say, "I built this wall; I earned this land by my labor." Someone could object: "Who marked it out for you, and what right have you to expect payment at our expense for doing what we never required of you? Do you not know that many of your brothers die or suffer badly for lack of what you have in excess of what nature requires, and that you needed the express and unanimous consent of mankind to take from the common stock more than you needed for your own living?" Lacking sound reasons to justify himself and enough force to defend himself, able to crush individuals easily but just as easily crushed by crowds, one man against all, and unable, because of mutual jealousies, to unite with his equals against bandits united by the shared hope of plunder, the rich man, driven by necessity, finally conceived the cleverest plan that ever entered the human mind. It was to use in his favor the very forces that attacked him, to make allies of his enemies, to instill other maxims in them and make them adopt other institutions as favorable to his claims as the law of nature was unfavorable.

With this aim, after setting before his neighbors all the horrors of a situation that armed them against one another, made their possessions as heavy as their needs were intolerable, and in which no one could expect any safety in either poverty or wealth, he easily devised plausible arguments to bring them round to his purpose. "Let us unite," he said, "to shield the weak from oppression, restrain the ambitious and secure for each man the possession of what belongs to him. Let us establish rules of justice and peace that everyone must follow, that favor no one, and that in some way make up for the whims of fortune by subjecting the powerful and the weak alike to mutual obligations. In a word, instead of turning our forces against ourselves, let us gather them into a supreme power that will govern us by sensible laws, protect and defend every member of the association, repel common enemies and maintain lasting harmony among us."

Far fewer words of this kind were enough to win over a crowd of rustics, who were easy to deceive, who had too many quarrels among themselves to live without arbiters, and too much greed and ambition to live long without masters. All of them offered their necks to the yoke in hope of securing their liberty. They had enough sense to see the advantages of a political constitution but not enough experience to foresee its dangers. Those among them best able to foresee the abuses were precisely those who expected to profit from them, and even the most sober judged it necessary to sacrifice one part of their liberty to protect the other, as a man with a badly wounded limb readily gives it up to save the rest of his body.

Such was, or must have been if man had been left to himself, the origin of society and of laws, which gave new fetters to the weak and new strength to the rich; irretrievably destroyed natural liberty; fixed forever the law of property and inequality; turned a clever usurpation into an irrevocable right; and, for the profit of a few ambitious individuals, subjected the rest of mankind to perpetual labor, servitude and misery. We can easily see how the establishment of a single society made the setting up of all the others necessary, and how, to face united forces, all remaining mankind had to band together in turn. Societies formed in this way soon multiplied and spread until they covered the face of the earth, leaving no corner of the universe where a man could throw off the yoke and pull his head from under the sword, often wielded badly, that he saw forever hanging over it. Civil law having thus become the common rule for citizens, the law of nature no longer held except between different societies, where, under the name of the law of nations, it was modified by tacit conventions to make trade possible and to take the place of natural compassion. Compassion, gradually losing in societies all the influence it originally had over individuals, now survives only in a few great souls who see themselves as citizens of the world and, breaking through the imaginary barriers that separate peoples, after the example of the Sovereign Being from whom we all derive our existence, make the whole human race the object of their goodwill.

Political bodies, thus remaining in a state of nature toward one another, soon experienced the troubles that had forced individuals to leave it, and that state proved much more fatal to these great bodies than it had been before to the individuals who now made them up. From this come those national wars, those battles, those murders, those reprisals that make nature shudder and shock reason; from this come all those horrible prejudices that make it a virtue and an honor to shed human blood. The worthiest men learned to regard cutting their fellows' throats as a duty; at length men began to slaughter one another by thousands without knowing why; and more murders were committed in a single battle, and more horrible disorders at the capture of a single town, than had been committed in the state of nature over ages together across the whole face of the earth. Such are the first effects we may suppose to have arisen from the division of mankind into different societies. Let us return to their institution.

I know that several writers have assigned other origins to political society, for instance the conquests of the powerful or the union of the weak, and it makes no difference to what I am about to establish which of these causes we adopt. Still, the one I have just set out seems to me the most natural, for these reasons. First, in the case of conquest, the right of conquest is in fact no right at all and so could not serve as the foundation of any other right; the conqueror and the conquered would always remain at war with one another, unless the conquered, restored to the full possession of their liberty, freely chose their conqueror as their chief. Until then, whatever agreements might have been made between them, since those agreements were based on violence and hence null and void in fact, there could not have existed under this hypothesis either a true society, or a political body, or any law besides that of the strongest. Second, in the case of the union of the weak, the words strong and weak are ambiguous. In the period between the establishment of the right of property or first occupation and that of political government, the meaning of these terms is better expressed by the words poor and rich, because before laws existed men in reality had no other means of subduing their equals than by attacking their property or by giving up some of their own to them. Third, since the poor had nothing to lose but their liberty, it would have been the height of madness for them to give up willingly the only good they had left without getting something in return. The rich, on the other hand, were vulnerable, so to speak, in every part of their possessions, so it was much easier to do them harm and they had more reason to guard against it. And finally, it is only reasonable to assume that a thing was devised by the one to whom it could be useful rather than by the one to whom it must prove harmful.

Government in its infancy had no regular or permanent form. For lack of enough philosophy and experience, men could see no further than present troubles and thought of providing remedies for future ones only as they arose. In spite of all the labors of the wisest lawgivers, the political state stayed imperfect because it was largely the work of chance; and since its foundations were badly laid, time, though enough to reveal its defects and suggest remedies, could never repair its original flaws. Men were constantly patching, whereas to build a good structure they should have begun, as Lycurgus did at Sparta, by clearing the ground and removing the old materials. At first society consisted merely of some general agreements that all members bound themselves to observe, and for whose fulfillment the whole body became guarantor to each individual. Experience was needed to show the great weakness of such a constitution, and how easy it was for those who broke it to escape conviction or punishment for faults of which the public alone was to be both witness and judge. The laws could not fail to be evaded in a thousand ways, and troubles and disorders could not help multiplying, until at last it was found necessary to think of entrusting private persons with the dangerous trust of public authority, and magistrates with the duty of enforcing the people's obedience. To say that chiefs were chosen before associations were formed, and that the ministers of the laws existed before the laws themselves, is a supposition too ridiculous for me to refute seriously.

It would be equally unreasonable to imagine that men at first threw themselves into the arms of an absolute master, without conditions or any return from him, and that the first means devised by jealous, unconquered men for their common safety was to rush headlong into slavery. Indeed, why did they give themselves superiors if not to be defended by them against oppression, and protected in their lives, liberties and properties, which are in a way the essential components of their being? Now, in the relations between man and man, the worst that can happen to anyone is to find himself at another's mercy. Would it not have been contrary to good sense to begin by handing over to a chief the only things for the protection of which they needed his help? What equivalent could he have offered them for so fine a privilege? And if he had dared to claim it on the pretext of protecting them, would he not at once have received the answer in the fable: "What worse can an enemy do to us?" It is thus beyond dispute, and indeed a fundamental maxim of political law, that people gave themselves chiefs to defend their liberty and not to be enslaved by them. "If we have a prince," said Pliny to Trajan, "it is so that he may keep us from having a master."

Political writers argue about the love of liberty with the same sophistry that philosophers use about the state of nature. From the things they see, they judge very different things they have never seen, and they attribute to men a natural inclination toward slavery because of the patience with which the slaves they know carry the yoke. They do not realize that liberty is like innocence and virtue: its worth is known only to those who possess it, and the taste for it is lost along with the thing itself. "I know the charms of your country," Brasidas said to a satrap who was comparing the life of the Spartans with that of the Persians, "but you cannot know the pleasures of mine."

As an unbroken colt bristles its mane, paws the ground and rages at the mere sight of the bit, while a trained horse patiently bears both whip and spur, so the barbarian will never bend his neck to the yoke that civilized man carries without complaint, but prefers the stormiest liberty to a peaceful subjection. So it is not by the servile attitude of enslaved nations that we should judge man's natural inclinations for or against slavery, but by the marvels every free people performs to protect itself from oppression. I know that the first group are always praising the peace and quiet they enjoy in their chains, and that miserrimam servitutem pacem appellant. But when I see the others sacrifice pleasures, peace, riches, power and even life itself to preserve that single treasure so scorned by those who have lost it; when I see animals born free dash out their brains against the bars of their cage out of a natural horror of captivity; when I see crowds of naked savages scorn European pleasures and defy hunger, fire, sword and death itself to keep their independence, I sense that it is not for slaves to reason about liberty.

As for paternal authority, from which several writers have derived absolute government and every other form of society, it is enough, without turning to Locke and Sidney, to observe that nothing in the world is more unlike the cruel spirit of despotism than the gentleness of that authority, which looks more to the benefit of the one who obeys than to the advantage of the one who commands. By the law of nature the father remains master of his child only as long as the child needs his help; after that they are equals, and the son, entirely independent of his father, owes him no obedience but only respect. Gratitude is indeed a duty we must pay, but one that benefactors cannot demand. Instead of saying that civil society derives from paternal authority, we should say rather that it is from civil society that paternal authority gets its main strength. No individual was recognized as the father of several others until they gathered around him. The father's goods, which he can indeed dispose of as he pleases, are the ties that hold his children in dependence on him, and he may divide his property among them in proportion to how well they have earned his regard by constant deference to his wishes. The subjects of a despotic chief, on the other hand, far from having any such favor to expect from him, since they themselves and all they have are his property, or at least are considered by him as such, are obliged to accept as a favor whatever he leaves them of their own belongings. He does them justice when he strips them; he shows them mercy when he lets them live.

If we keep comparing fact with right in this way, we will find as little soundness as truth in the voluntary founding of tyranny. It would be hard to prove the validity of a contract that binds only one side, in which one party stakes everything and the other nothing, and which could only turn out to the harm of the one who bound himself. This odious system is even today far from being that of wise and good monarchs, and especially of the kings of France, as can be seen from various passages in their edicts, and particularly from a celebrated document published in 1667 in the name and by the orders of Louis XIV: "Let it not be said, then, that the sovereign is not subject to the laws of his realm, since that he is, is a maxim of the law of nations which flattery has sometimes attacked but which good princes have always defended as the guardian deity of their realms. How much more reasonable is it to say, with wise Plato, that the perfect happiness of a state consists in the subjects obeying their prince, the prince obeying the laws, and the laws being fair and always directed to the public good? I will not stop to consider whether, liberty being man's noblest faculty, it is not demeaning one's nature, reducing oneself to the rank of the brutes that are slaves of instinct, and even offending the Author of one's being, to renounce without reserve the most precious of his gifts and to submit to committing all the crimes he has forbidden us merely to please a mad or cruel master; and whether this sublime Craftsman ought to be more angered at seeing his work destroyed than at seeing it dishonored. I will only ask what right those who did not shrink from degrade themselves this way could have to subject their descendants to the same disgrace, and to renounce, in the name of their posterity, blessings that it does not owe to their generosity and without which life itself must seem a burden to all who are worthy to live."

Pufendorf says that, as we can transfer our property to others by contracts and agreements, we may likewise strip ourselves of our freedom in favor of other men. This, in my opinion, is very poor reasoning. To begin with, the property I give to another becomes by that transfer something quite foreign to me, whose misuse cannot affect me; but it matters greatly to me that my liberty is not misused, and I cannot, without taking on the guilt of the crimes I might be forced to commit, expose myself to becoming the instrument of any. Besides, the right of property being a matter of merely human convention and institution, every man may dispose as he pleases of what he owns. But the case is different for the essential gifts of nature, such as life and liberty, which every man is allowed to enjoy and which it is doubtful, at least, that anyone has the right to give up. By giving up the one we degrade our being; by giving up the other we destroy it as far as it is in our power to do so; and since no worldly enjoyment can make up for losing either, it would offend both nature and reason to renounce them for any price. But even supposing we could transfer our freedom as we do our goods, the difference would be very great for our children, who enjoy our property only by a transfer of our right, whereas liberty, being a blessing they hold from nature as human beings, cannot be taken from them by their parents. So just as it took violence to nature to establish slavery, it took altering nature to perpetuate that right; and the jurists who have gravely pronounced that the child of a slave is born a slave have in other words decided that a man is not born a man.

It therefore appears to me incontestably true not only that governments did not begin with arbitrary power, which is but the corruption and extreme end of government and eventually brings it back to the law of the strongest, for which governments were at first the remedy, but also that, even supposing they had begun in this way, such power, being illegitimate in itself, could never have served as the foundation for the rights of society, nor consequently for the inequality of institution.

I will not now enter into the inquiries that remain to be made about the nature of the fundamental pacts of each kind of government. Following the common opinion, I will limit myself here to treating the establishment of the political body as a real contract between the multitude and the chiefs it chooses. By this contract both sides commit themselves to observe the laws it stipulates, which form the bonds of their union. The multitude, having on the occasion of their social relations gathered all their wills into one person, makes every article on which that will declares itself into a fundamental law, binding without exception on all members of the state. One of these laws regulates the choice and powers of the magistrates appointed to oversee the carrying out of the rest. This authority extends to everything that can maintain the constitution but to nothing that could alter it. Honors are added to it, to make the laws and their ministers respected, and the persons of the ministers are distinguished by certain privileges to compensate them for the heavy labors that come with good administration. The magistrate for his part commits himself to use the power given to him only in accordance with the intentions of those who gave it, to maintain each of them in peaceful possession of his property, and on every occasion to prefer the public good to his own private interest.

Before experience had shown, or a thorough knowledge of the human heart had pointed out, the abuses inseparable from such a constitution, it must have seemed all the more perfect because those charged with preserving it were themselves most concerned in it. For since the magistracy and its rights rest solely on the fundamental laws, as soon as those ceased to exist the magistrates would cease to be legitimate, the people would no longer be bound to obey them, and, since the essence of the state did not lie in the magistrates but in the laws, its members would immediately regain their primitive and natural liberty.

A little reflection would give us new arguments confirming this truth, and the nature of the contract alone might convince us that it cannot be irrevocable. If there were no higher power able to guarantee the good faith of the contracting parties and force them to fulfill their mutual commitments, they would remain sole judges in their own case, and each would always have the right to withdraw from the contract once he found that the other had broken its terms, or that those terms had ceased to suit his private convenience. On this principle the right of abdication may probably be founded. Now, if we consider, as we do, only what is human in this institution, then if the magistrate, who has all the power in his own hands and who takes for himself all the advantages of the contract, nevertheless has the right to give up his authority, how much better a right must the people have, who pay for all the faults of their chief, to renounce their dependence on him. But the shocking dissensions and countless disorders that would necessarily follow from so perilous a privilege show, above all else, how much human governments needed a firmer basis than reason alone, and how necessary it was for public peace that the will of the Almighty should step in to give sovereign authority a sacred and inviolable character, depriving subjects of the harmful right to dispose of it as they pleased. If mankind had gained no other advantage from religion, this alone would be enough to make them adopt and cherish it, since it saves more blood than fanaticism has ever spilled. But let us pick up the thread of our hypothesis again.

The various forms of government owe their origin to the various degrees of inequality among the members at the moment they first merged into a political body. Where one man happened to stand out for power, virtue, wealth or influence, he became the only magistrate, and the state took a monarchical form. If several of fairly equal eminence rose above all the rest, they were elected jointly, and this election produced an aristocracy. Those between whose fortunes or talents there was no such disproportion, and who had strayed less far from the state of nature, kept the supreme administration in common and formed a democracy. Time showed which of these forms suited mankind best. Some remained wholly subject to the laws; others soon bowed their necks to masters. The former worked to preserve their liberty; the latter thought of nothing but taking their neighbors', jealous at seeing others enjoy a blessing they had lost themselves. In a word, riches and conquest fell to the share of one, and virtue and happiness to the other.

In these various forms of government, all offices were at first elective. When wealth did not predominate, preference was given to merit, which gives a natural authority, and to age, which is the parent of deliberation in council and experience in execution. The elders of the Hebrews, the Gerontes of Sparta, the Senate of Rome, and even the very origin of our word seigneur show how much gray hair was once respected. The more often the choice fell on old men, the more often it had to be repeated, and the more the trouble of these repetitions was felt. Electioneering set in; factions arose; the parties grew bitter; civil wars blazed up; the lives of citizens were sacrificed to the alleged happiness of the state; and things finally reached the point of nearly falling back into their original confusion. The ambition of the leading men led them to take advantage of these circumstances to make the hitherto temporary offices permanent in their families. The people, already used to dependence, accustomed to ease and the comforts of life, and too softened to break their fetters, agreed to an increase in their slavery in order to secure their peace. In this way chiefs became hereditary, and acquired the habit of regarding magistracies as a family estate and themselves as owners of the communities in which they were at first mere officers; of calling their fellow citizens their slaves; of counting them, like so many cows or sheep, as part of their property; and of styling themselves the peers of gods and kings of kings.

By following the progress of inequality through these different revolutions, we will find that the establishment of laws and the right of property was the first stage, the establishment of magistrates the second, and the third and last the change from legitimate to arbitrary power. So the different conditions of rich and poor were authorized by the first period, those of powerful and weak by the second, and by the third those of master and slave, which formed the last degree of inequality and the point at which all the rest finally end, until new revolutions either dissolve the government completely or bring it back closer to its legitimate constitution.

To understand the necessity of this progress, we should consider not so much the reasons for establishing political bodies as the forms these bodies take in their administration and the troubles that essentially come with them. For the very vices that make social institutions necessary also make the abuse of those institutions unavoidable. And since the laws, which are in general weaker than the passions, restrain men without changing them (Sparta alone excepted, whose laws mainly concerned the education of children, and where Lycurgus established such manners and customs as largely made laws unnecessary), it would not be hard to prove that every government which, guarding carefully against all alteration and corruption, scrupulously fulfilled the purposes of its institution, was instituted needlessly, and that a country where no one evaded the laws or misused the magistracy would need neither laws nor magistrates.

Political distinctions necessarily bring civil distinctions with them. The inequality between the people and the chiefs grows so fast that private members soon feel it, and it appears among them in a thousand forms according to their passions, talents and circumstances. The magistrate cannot usurp any illegitimate power without making dependents for himself, with whom he must share it. Besides, the citizens of a free state let themselves be oppressed only in proportion as blind ambition carries them away and, looking down rather than up, they come to love authority more than independence. When they submit to fetters, it is only to be better able to fetter others in their turn. It is hard to make a man obey who does not wish to command, and the most refined policy would find it impossible to subdue men who only want to be independent. But inequality easily gains ground among base and ambitious souls, always ready to run the risks of fortune and almost indifferent whether they command or obey, according to whether she favors or opposes them. So there must have been a time when the people's eyes were so bewitched that their rulers needed only say to the most pitiful wretch, "Be great, you and all your descendants," for him at once to look great in everyone's eyes as well as his own. His descendants took even more on themselves the further they were removed from him; the more distant and uncertain the cause, the greater the effect; the longer the line of idlers a family produced, the more illustrious it was thought.

If this were the place for details, I could easily explain how inequalities of influence and authority become unavoidable among individuals as soon as, united in one body, they are forced to compare themselves with one another and to notice the differences they find in the constant use each must make of his neighbors. These differences take several forms. But wealth, noble rank, power and personal merit are in general the main distinctions by which men in society measure each other, and I could prove that the harmony or conflict among these different forces is the surest sign of a state's good or bad original constitution.
